sk: अन्यच्छ्रेयोऽन्यदुतैव प्रेयस्ते उभे नानार्थे पुरुषं सिनीतः | तयोः श्रेय आददानस्य साधु भवति हीयतेऽर्थाद्य उ प्रेयो वृणीते ||
ro: anyac · chreyaḥ · anyad · utaiva · preyaḥ · te · ubhe · nānārthe · puruṣaṁ · sinītaḥ | tayoḥ · śreya · ādadānasya · sādhu · bhavati · hīyate · arthād · ya · u · preyo · vṛṇīte ||
hi: श्रेय (कल्याणकारी) और है, प्रेय (प्रिय लगने वाला) और है — ये दोनों भिन्न-भिन्न लक्ष्यों वाले हैं और पुरुष को बाँधते हैं। इनमें से जो श्रेय को ग्रहण करता है उसका कल्याण होता है; जो प्रेय को चुनता है वह अपने वास्तविक लक्ष्य से भ्रष्ट हो जाता है।
en: The good (śreyas) is one thing; the pleasant (preyas) is another. Both, having different ends, bind a person. It goes well with the one who chooses the good; the one who chooses the pleasant falls from the true aim.

ws.e: the good, the beneficial — comparative of √śrī; that which leads to ultimate well-being
the pleasant, the agreeable — comparative of √prī; what is immediately gratifying
having different purposes — nānā (different) + artha (aim, purpose)
bind — 3rd dual present of √si ('to bind'); both paths entangle the person

ws.h: गिर जाता है, भ्रष्ट होता है
ws.e: falls away, is diminished — passive of √hā ('to leave, abandon'); loses the true goal

gr: śreyaḥ / preyaḥ — both are comparatives (not superlatives), suggesting a choice between 'better' and 'more pleasing,' not absolute good and evil. sinītaḥ — dual number verb: both paths actively bind; neither leaves the person free until the choice is made. hīyate arthāt — 'falls from the purpose': not punished externally but self-diminished by choosing wrongly.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.1 — This is the foundational ethical teaching of the Katha Upanishad. Yama distinguishes two fundamental orientations: śreyas (the path of liberation) and preyas (the path of gratification). This maps onto the Gita's later distinction between sāttvic and rājasic temperaments.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि श्रेय विद्या (ज्ञान) का मार्ग है और प्रेय अविद्या (अज्ञान) का। श्रेय मोक्ष की ओर ले जाता है, प्रेय संसार-बन्धन को और दृढ़ करता है। नचिकेता ने श्रेय चुनकर ज्ञान का अधिकारी होने की योग्यता प्रमाणित की।
advaita.en: Shankara identifies śreyas with vidyā (knowledge) and preyas with avidyā (ignorance). Śreyas leads to mokṣa; preyas reinforces saṁsāric bondage. Nachiketa proved his fitness for knowledge by choosing śreyas.
advaita.ins: The capacity to distinguish between what is truly good and what merely feels good is the first qualification of a spiritual seeker.

vishisht.h: रामानुज के अनुसार श्रेय भगवान् की ओर ले जाने वाला मार्ग है और प्रेय इन्द्रिय-विषयों में फँसाने वाला। भगवान् की कृपा से ही मनुष्य श्रेय को पहचान पाता है — नचिकेता पर यही कृपा थी।
vishisht.en: For Ramanuja, śreyas is the path leading to the Lord and preyas is entanglement in sense-objects. Only by the Lord's grace can one recognise śreyas — this grace was upon Nachiketa.
vishisht.ins: The very ability to prefer the eternal over the ephemeral is itself a sign of divine grace working within the seeker.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द श्रेय को उच्चतर चेतना की पुकार और प्रेय को निम्नतर प्रकृति के आकर्षण के रूप में देखते हैं। यह द्वन्द्व मनुष्य की आन्तरिक लड़ाई है — आत्मा का आह्वान बनाम अहंकार का खिंचाव।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees śreyas as the call of the higher consciousness and preyas as the attraction of the lower nature. This duality is the inner battle of the human being — the soul's summons versus the ego's pull.
aurobindo.ins: Evolution demands choosing the harder path repeatedly. Each choice of śreyas over preyas is a step in the soul's ascent.

dp.q: 🔍 How do śreyas and preyas differ from good and evil?
dp.a: The śreyas/preyas distinction is subtler than a simple good/evil binary. Both are comparatives — 'more beneficial' and 'more pleasing' — not absolutes. Preyas is not evil; it is genuinely pleasant and attractive. A delicious meal, a comfortable life, even heaven — these are preyas. They are real goods, but they are lesser goods. Śreyas is what serves one's ultimate well-being — it may be difficult, uncomfortable, even painful in the moment. The Upanishad does not say preyas is sinful; it says one who chooses it hīyate arthāt — 'falls from the purpose.' The tragedy is not punishment but the quiet loss of one's highest possibility. This is why Yama's temptations to Nachiketa (in the previous Valli) were all genuine goods — long life, wealth, power — not vices.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Yama begin his teaching here and not with metaphysics?
dp.a: Yama's teaching strategy is deliberate: he begins with ethics before metaphysics. Before revealing the nature of the Atman, he establishes the prerequisite — the capacity for right choice. The Katha Upanishad is structured as a progressive revelation: first, the seeker must demonstrate fitness (Valli 1, the temptation test); then the teacher validates that fitness and establishes the framework of discernment (this verse); only then does the teaching of the Self unfold. This mirrors the traditional four qualifications (sādhana-catuṣṭaya) in Advaita: viveka (discrimination), vairāgya (dispassion), ṣaṭ-sampatti (six virtues), and mumukṣutva (desire for liberation). Nachiketa has demonstrated all four — now he is ready to receive.

sk: श्रेयश्च प्रेयश्च मनुष्यमेतस्तौ सम्परीत्य विविनक्ति धीरः | श्रेयो हि धीरोऽभि प्रेयसो वृणीते प्रेयो मन्दो योगक्षेमाद्वृणीते ||
ro: śreyaś · ca · preyaś · ca · manuṣyam · etas · tau · samparītya · vivinakti · dhīraḥ | śreyo · hi · dhīraḥ · abhi · preyaso · vṛṇīte · preyo · mando · yogakṣemād · vṛṇīte ||
hi: श्रेय और प्रेय दोनों मनुष्य के पास आते हैं। धीर (विवेकशील) पुरुष उन दोनों को परख कर अलग-अलग पहचान लेता है। धीर पुरुष प्रेय की अपेक्षा श्रेय को चुनता है; मन्द (अविवेकी) पुरुष योगक्षेम (लाभ और रक्षा) के लोभ से प्रेय को चुनता है।
en: Both the good and the pleasant approach a person. The wise one examines and distinguishes between them. The wise chooses the good over the pleasant; the dull-witted chooses the pleasant for the sake of worldly gain and security.

ws.h: चारों ओर से घेर कर, परख कर
ws.e: having gone around, having examined — absolutive of sam+pari+√i; implies thorough examination

ws.h: पृथक् करता है, भेद करता है
ws.e: discriminates, separates — vi+vi+√naj; the root sense is 'to sift apart'
the wise, the steadfast — from √dhī ('to think, reflect'); one with firm understanding
the dull, the slow-witted — one who lacks discernment

ws.h: योग (अप्राप्त की प्राप्ति) और क्षेम (प्राप्त की रक्षा) के कारण
ws.e: for the sake of acquisition and preservation — yoga (gaining what is not had) + kṣema (keeping what is had)

gr: samparītya vivinakti — 'having gone around them, separates': the wise person does not impulsively choose; they examine both options from all sides before discriminating. yogakṣemāt — a compound capturing the two basic drives of worldly life: acquiring (yoga) and preserving (kṣema). The manda chooses preyas because it serves these immediate concerns. dhīraḥ/mandaḥ — the contrast is not moral but intellectual: wisdom versus dullness of perception.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.2 — The dhīra/manda contrast introduces the epistemic dimension: the difference is not in virtue but in clarity of vision. Yogakṣema anticipates the Gita (9.22) where Krishna promises yogakṣema to the devoted — but here it is what the unwise cling to.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'विविनक्ति' (भेद करना) ही विवेक है — अनित्य से नित्य को अलग करने की बुद्धि। यही सम्पूर्ण वेदान्त-साधना का प्रथम सोपान है। मन्द पुरुष में यह विवेक-शक्ति सुप्त रहती है।
advaita.en: Shankara identifies 'vivinakti' (discriminates) as viveka — the intellect that separates the eternal from the non-eternal. This is the first step of the entire Vedantic discipline. In the manda, this faculty of discrimination remains dormant.
advaita.ins: Viveka is not a learned skill but an awakened faculty. The entire spiritual path begins with the simple act of seeing clearly what is real and what is passing.

vishisht.h: रामानुज के अनुसार धीर वह है जिसे भगवान् ने विवेक-बुद्धि प्रदान की है। मन्द अपनी बुद्धि से नहीं बल्कि इन्द्रियों से संचालित होता है। भगवान् की शरणागति ही मन्द को धीर बनाने का उपाय है।
vishisht.en: For Ramanuja, the dhīra is one to whom the Lord has granted the faculty of discernment. The manda is driven not by intellect but by senses. Surrender to the Lord is the means by which the manda becomes dhīra.
vishisht.ins: Discernment is a divine gift, not merely an intellectual achievement. Seeking it through prayer and surrender is itself a form of wisdom.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'योगक्षेम' को अहंकार की मूल प्रवृत्ति मानते हैं — पाना और पकड़े रहना। धीर वह है जो इस प्रवृत्ति से ऊपर उठ कर आत्मा की पुकार सुनता है। मन्द इसी प्रवृत्ति में बँधा रहता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees 'yogakṣema' as the ego's fundamental drive — to acquire and to hold. The dhīra is one who rises above this drive to hear the soul's call. The manda remains trapped in it.
aurobindo.ins: The soul's evolution requires transcending the survival instinct of the ego. The wise person risks present comfort for a future that the ego cannot even imagine.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'vivinakti' reveal about the nature of wisdom?
dp.a: The word vivinakti (from vi+vi+√naj, 'to sift apart') is extraordinarily precise. It is the same root from which viveka (discrimination) derives. The verb implies a physical act of separating grain from chaff — the wise person does not reject preyas out of ascetic disgust but carefully sifts the two apart. This means both śreyas and preyas may appear mixed together in life's offerings; they are not always obviously different. The dhīra's skill lies in detecting the subtle difference — recognising when apparent good is actually pleasant-dressed-as-good, and when apparent difficulty is actually the truly beneficial path. Samparītya (having gone around) adds that this examination is thorough — from all sides, not a snap judgment.

dp.q: 🔍 What is yogakṣema and why is it the manda's trap?
dp.a: Yogakṣema is a compound of two concerns: yoga (not the spiritual practice but literally 'acquisition' — gaining what one does not have) and kṣema ('security' — preserving what one has gained). Together they capture the entire anxiety of worldly life: getting and keeping. The manda chooses preyas not because they are evil but because preyas serves these two drives. Every pleasant choice promises either gain or safety. The tragedy is that this is reasonable from the ego's perspective — but it forecloses the possibility of transformation. In the Bhagavad Gita (9.22), Krishna promises 'yogakṣemaṁ vahāmy aham' — 'I carry their yogakṣema' — to those who surrender completely. The Gita's solution is not to eliminate the need for security but to transfer it from the ego to the Divine.

sk: स त्वं प्रियान् प्रियरूपांश्च कामानभिध्यायन् नचिकेतोऽत्यस्राक्षीः | नैतां सृङ्कां वित्तमयीमवाप्तो यस्यां मज्जन्ति बहवो मनुष्याः ||
ro: sa · tvaṁ · priyān · priyarūpāṁś · ca · kāmān · abhidhyāyan · naciketo · atyasrākṣīḥ | na · etāṁ · sṛṅkāṁ · vittamayīm · avāpto · yasyāṁ · majjanti · bahavo · manuṣyāḥ ||
hi: हे नचिकेता! तूने प्रिय वस्तुओं को और प्रिय रूपों वाली कामनाओं को भली-भाँति विचार कर त्याग दिया। तू इस धन-सम्पत्ति की उस श्रृंखला (जंजीर) में नहीं फँसा जिसमें बहुत से मनुष्य डूब जाते हैं।
en: You, O Nachiketa, having reflected upon the desirable and the desire-worthy pleasures, have cast them aside. You have not entered this chain of wealth in which many human beings sink and drown.

ws.e: the dear, the desirable things — accusative plural; the temptations Yama offered
having pleasing forms — the attractiveness of the objects themselves
having contemplated, having reflected deeply — present participle of abhi+√dhyai
cast aside, let go — aorist of ati+√sṛj ('to release beyond'); a decisive, completed rejection
chain, fetter — the image of wealth as a chain that binds
made of wealth — vitta (wealth) + mayī (made of, consisting of)
sink, drown — √majj ('to sink'); they don't just fall but go under completely

gr: abhidhyāyan — 'having contemplated': Nachiketa's rejection was not impulsive but considered. He saw the pleasures clearly and still chose to let them go. atyasrākṣīḥ — aorist of ati+√sṛj: 'released beyond'; a decisive, irreversible casting aside. sṛṅkāṁ vittamayīm — 'chain made of wealth': wealth is not a reward but a fetter. The image is startling — gold becomes a chain, possessions become prison. majjanti — 'they drown': not a gentle metaphor; most people go completely under.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.3 — Yama validates Nachiketa's choice from Valli 1. The striking image of wealth as a sṛṅkā (chain/fetter) inverts the common assumption — possessions do not free, they bind. The word majjanti (drown) suggests a spiritual death more final than physical death.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'अभिध्यायन्' (विचारपूर्वक) शब्द दर्शाता है कि नचिकेता का त्याग अज्ञान से नहीं, ज्ञान से हुआ — उसने कामनाओं को जानकर छोड़ा। यही वैराग्य की सर्वोच्च कोटि है — जो देखकर भी न फँसे।
advaita.en: Shankara notes that 'abhidhyāyan' (having contemplated) shows Nachiketa's renunciation was born of knowledge, not ignorance — he knew what he was giving up. This is the highest grade of vairāgya — seeing and still not being caught.
advaita.ins: True renunciation is not turning away from what you don't know, but letting go of what you fully understand to be attractive yet ultimately binding.

vishisht.h: रामानुज के अनुसार नचिकेता ने भगवान् की कृपा से सांसारिक सुखों की तुच्छता देखी। 'वित्तमयी सृङ्का' — धन की जंजीर — भगवान् से विमुख करने वाली सबसे बड़ी बाधा है।
vishisht.en: For Ramanuja, Nachiketa saw the insignificance of worldly pleasures through the Lord's grace. 'Vittamayī sṛṅkā' — the chain of wealth — is the greatest obstacle to turning toward the Lord.
vishisht.ins: Wealth is not evil in itself, but attachment to it becomes the strongest chain binding the soul from its divine source.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'सृङ्का' (जंजीर) के रूपक में भौतिक चेतना के बन्धन देखते हैं। धन केवल धातु या मुद्रा नहीं — यह एक चेतना-अवस्था है जो मनुष्य को शरीर और इन्द्रियों के स्तर पर बाँधे रखती है। नचिकेता ने इस स्तर को पार किया।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads the 'sṛṅkā' (chain) metaphor as the bondage of material consciousness. Wealth is not just metal or currency — it is a state of consciousness that keeps the human bound to the level of body and senses. Nachiketa transcended this level.
aurobindo.ins: What we own ends up owning us — not because possessions are evil but because they anchor consciousness at the material level.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Yama praise Nachiketa before teaching him?
dp.a: Yama's praise in this verse serves a specific pedagogical function: establishing adhikāra (qualification). In the Vedantic tradition, not everyone is fit to receive the highest teaching. The teacher must verify that the student has the necessary preparation — especially viveka (discrimination) and vairāgya (dispassion). By explicitly acknowledging Nachiketa's rejection of temptations ('you cast aside the pleasant... you did not enter the chain of wealth'), Yama is formally recognising him as an adhikārī — a qualified student. This is not flattery; it is a necessary preliminary. Without this recognition, the subsequent teaching about the Atman would be premature. The structure mirrors the traditional guru-śiṣya relationship: the teacher tests, the student passes, the teacher acknowledges, and only then does the teaching begin.

dp.q: 🔍 What does the image of wealth as a 'chain' (sṛṅkā) mean?
dp.a: The word sṛṅkā (chain, fetter) is deliberately provocative. In ordinary perception, wealth represents freedom — the ability to do what one wants, go where one pleases, live as one chooses. Yama inverts this: wealth is a chain, and those who grasp it majjanti (drown). The image works on two levels: (1) Practically — wealth demands maintenance, protection, increase; the wealthy person becomes servant to their possessions. (2) Spiritually — attachment to wealth anchors consciousness in the material plane, making it impossible to inquire into what lies beyond. The compound vittamayīm ('made of wealth') is precise — the chain is not around the wealth but composed of it. Each possession is a link. The more you accumulate, the heavier the chain.

sk: दूरमेते विपरीते विषूची अविद्या या च विद्येति ज्ञाता | विद्याभीप्सिनं नचिकेतसं मन्ये न त्वा कामा बहवोऽलोलुपन्त ||
ro: dūram · ete · viparīte · viṣūcī · avidyā · yā · ca · vidyā · iti · jñātā | vidyā · abhīpsinaṁ · naciketasaṁ · manye · na · tvā · kāmā · bahavo · alolupanta ||
hi: ये दोनों — अविद्या और विद्या — एक-दूसरे से दूर, विपरीत दिशाओं में जाने वाली, और भिन्न-भिन्न हैं — ऐसा जानी जाती हैं। मैं नचिकेता को विद्या का अभिलाषी मानता हूँ — तुझे बहुत-सी कामनाओं ने विचलित नहीं किया।
en: Widely apart and leading in opposite directions are these two — ignorance (avidyā) and what is known as knowledge (vidyā). I consider Nachiketa to be a seeker of knowledge — the many desires did not tempt you.

ws.e: opposed, contrary — going in diametrically opposite directions
diverging — from vi+√sūc; they lead to entirely different destinations
ignorance — not mere absence of knowledge but active mis-knowing; taking the unreal for real
knowledge — specifically liberating knowledge (ātma-vidyā); not mere information
desiring, seeking — from abhi+√āp (desiderative); one who intensely seeks to attain

ws.h: लुभा न सके, विचलित न कर सके
ws.e: did not make greedy, did not tempt — negative aorist of √lup (intensive); failed to create avarice

gr: dūram ete viparīte viṣūcī — three words piled to stress separation: 'far apart,' 'opposite,' 'diverging.' Avidyā and vidyā are not slightly different but utterly incompatible. alolupanta — intensive (frequentative) form of √lup: not merely 'did not attract' but 'did not make you repeatedly greedy.' The temptations were persistent; Nachiketa's resistance was firm.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.4 — Yama maps the śreyas/preyas distinction onto the vidyā/avidyā framework. This is a key link between ethical choice and epistemology — right choice requires right knowledge, and right knowledge produces right choice. The Isha Upanishad (9-11) also treats vidyā and avidyā as complementary; here they are presented as opposed.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि अविद्या-विद्या का यह भेद सम्पूर्ण वेदान्त का मूल है। अविद्या = अनात्मा को आत्मा मानना; विद्या = आत्मा को जानना। ये दो मार्ग 'विषूची' (विपरीत गामी) हैं — एक बन्धन की ओर, दूसरा मुक्ति की ओर।
advaita.en: Shankara says the avidyā/vidyā distinction is the foundation of all Vedanta. Avidyā = mistaking the non-Self for the Self; vidyā = knowing the Self. These two paths are 'viṣūcī' (diverging) — one toward bondage, the other toward liberation.
advaita.ins: The root of all suffering is a case of mistaken identity — taking what we are not (body, mind, ego) for what we truly are (Atman).

vishisht.h: रामानुज विद्या को भगवान् का ज्ञान और अविद्या को भगवान् से विमुखता मानते हैं। ये दोनों 'दूरम्' (बहुत दूर) हैं — भक्त और विषयी में आकाश-पाताल का अन्तर है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja reads vidyā as knowledge of the Lord and avidyā as turning away from the Lord. These two are 'dūram' (far apart) — the difference between the devotee and the worldling is as vast as heaven and earth.
vishisht.ins: To know God is to be oriented toward truth; to be ignorant of God is not neutral but actively misdirected.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द अविद्या को निम्नतर प्रकृति की चेतना और विद्या को उच्चतर चेतना (सुप्रामेंटल) की ओर बढ़ना मानते हैं। ये दो चेतना-धाराएँ 'विषूची' — विपरीत दिशाओं में बहती हैं। नचिकेता ने ऊर्ध्वगामी धारा को चुना।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads avidyā as the consciousness of the lower nature and vidyā as the movement toward higher (supramental) consciousness. These two streams of consciousness are 'viṣūcī' — flowing in opposite directions. Nachiketa chose the ascending stream.
aurobindo.ins: Every moment of awareness is either ascending toward truth-consciousness or descending into the inertia of matter. There is no neutral ground.

dp.q: 🔍 How does vidyā differ from ordinary knowledge?
dp.a: In the Upanishadic context, vidyā does not mean general learning, scholarship, or even intellectual brilliance. It means specifically ātma-vidyā — knowledge of the Self. The Mundaka Upanishad (1.1.4-5) makes the distinction explicit: aparā vidyā (lower knowledge) includes the four Vedas, grammar, astronomy, and all sciences; parā vidyā (higher knowledge) is 'that by which the Imperishable (akṣara) is known.' A person may have encyclopedic knowledge of every subject and still be in avidyā if they do not know the Self. Conversely, the simplest person who directly knows 'I am the Atman' possesses vidyā. This is why Yama calls Nachiketa — a boy, not a scholar — 'vidyābhīpsinam' (seeker of vidyā). The boy's qualification is not learning but the purity and intensity of his seeking.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the relationship between the śreyas/preyas and vidyā/avidyā pairs?
dp.a: Yama presents two parallel pairs that map onto each other: śreyas = vidyā (the good = knowledge) and preyas = avidyā (the pleasant = ignorance). But the mapping reveals something deeper: choosing the pleasant is not merely an ethical failure but an epistemological one. The person who chooses preyas does so because they do not see clearly — they mistake the transient for the permanent, the body for the Self, pleasure for fulfilment. Conversely, the person who sees clearly (vidyā) naturally chooses śreyas — not through will-power but through vision. This means ethics and epistemology are inseparable in the Upanishadic framework. You cannot know the truth and choose wrongly, because wrong choice is the symptom of not-knowing. This is also why Yama's 'teaching' is not moral instruction but a revelation of reality — once Nachiketa sees, the right choice will follow naturally.

sk: अविद्यायामन्तरे वर्तमानाः स्वयं धीराः पण्डितंमन्यमानाः | दन्द्रम्यमाणाः परियन्ति मूढा अन्धेनैव नीयमाना यथान्धाः ||
ro: avidyāyām · antare · vartamānāḥ · svayaṁ · dhīrāḥ · paṇḍitaṁmanyamānāḥ | dandramyamāṇāḥ · pariyanti · mūḍhāḥ · andhena · eva · nīyamānā · yathā · andhāḥ ||
hi: अविद्या के बीच में रहते हुए, अपने-आप को धीर और पण्डित मानते हुए, वे मूढ़ जन इधर-उधर भटकते हैं — जैसे अन्धे अन्धों द्वारा ले जाये जाते हैं।
en: Dwelling in the midst of ignorance, yet fancying themselves wise and learned, the deluded go round and round, staggering, like the blind led by the blind.

ws.e: in the midst of — locative; they are inside ignorance, surrounded by it
thinking themselves learned — paṇḍita + manyamāna; self-proclaimed scholars
wandering, staggering — intensive/frequentative of √dram; aimless, repeated movement

ws.h: चक्कर लगाते हैं, भ्रमण करते हैं
ws.e: go round and round — pari+√i; circular, never-arriving motion
deluded — past passive participle of √muh ('to be confused'); they are not merely ignorant but actively deluded

ws.s: अन्धेन नीयमानाः यथा अन्धाः (andhena nīyamānā yathā andhāḥ)
ws.h: जैसे अन्धे द्वारा ले जाये जाने वाले अन्धे
ws.e: like the blind led by the blind — the famous simile; the guides are as lost as the guided

gr: paṇḍitaṁmanyamānāḥ — a compound participle: 'thinking-themselves-learned.' The compound itself is the diagnosis — the delusion is not that they lack knowledge but that they believe they have it. dandramyamāṇāḥ — intensive (frequentative) of √dram: not walking but staggering, lurching, going to and fro without direction. pariyanti — 'go around': circular motion, never progressing. andhena nīyamānā yathā andhāḥ — the 'blind leading the blind' simile appears here centuries before its appearance in other traditions.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.5 — The 'blind leading the blind' is one of the most famous images in world literature. In context, Yama targets not the uneducated but the self-proclaimed scholars — those who teach what they do not understand. The Mundaka Upanishad (1.2.8) repeats this critique almost verbatim.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'पण्डितंमन्यमानाः' — अपने को विद्वान् मानने वाले — सबसे कठिन रोगी हैं। जो अज्ञानी जानता है कि वह अज्ञानी है, उसे सिखाया जा सकता है; जो अज्ञानी अपने को ज्ञानी मानता है, वह असाध्य है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'paṇḍitaṁmanyamānāḥ' — those who consider themselves learned — are the most difficult cases. An ignorant person who knows they are ignorant can be taught; an ignorant person who thinks they are wise is incurable.
advaita.ins: The greatest obstacle to awakening is not ignorance but the illusion of knowledge. Intellectual pride is harder to overcome than any sensual temptation.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि बिना भगवत्-कृपा के सारा पांडित्य अन्धकार ही है। 'अन्धेन नीयमानाः अन्धाः' — जो स्वयं भगवान् को नहीं जानता, वह दूसरों को क्या सिखाएगा? केवल भगवान् ही सच्चे गुरु हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja states that without the Lord's grace, all scholarship is darkness. 'The blind led by the blind' — one who does not know the Lord himself, what can he teach others? Only the Lord is the true guru.
vishisht.ins: A teacher without divine experience is like a lamp without oil — the form is there but the light is absent.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द इसमें मानसिक ज्ञान की सीमा देखते हैं — बुद्धि (mind) अविद्या के भीतर रहकर भी अपने को 'पण्डित' मान लेती है। असली ज्ञान बुद्धि से ऊपर — सुप्रामेंटल चेतना में — है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees here the limitation of mental knowledge — the mind (buddhi), while remaining within ignorance, can convince itself it is 'paṇḍita.' True knowledge lies above the mind — in supramental consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The mind is the greatest trickster: it can build elaborate systems of thought that are internally consistent yet entirely miss the truth. Real knowledge requires a faculty beyond mind.

dp.q: 🔍 Who are the 'blind leading the blind' in the Upanishadic context?
dp.a: The 'blind leading the blind' (andhena nīyamānā yathā andhāḥ) targets a specific class: ritual specialists and intellectual scholars who have mastered the external forms of religion without understanding their inner meaning. In the Upanishadic milieu, this critique was revolutionary. The Brahmins who performed elaborate Vedic rituals — fire sacrifices, soma ceremonies, complex liturgies — were the religious establishment. Yama is saying that even their expertise, if it lacks knowledge of the Self (ātma-vidyā), is a form of blindness. The Mundaka Upanishad (1.2.7-8) makes this even more explicit, calling ritualists who think heaven is the highest goal 'fools who praise each other' and condemning them to fall back from heaven when their merit is exhausted. This is the Upanishadic revolution: knowledge of the Self supersedes all ritual expertise.

dp.q: 🔍 What makes the 'staggering' (dandramyamāṇāḥ) image so powerful?
dp.a: The verb dandramyamāṇāḥ is a frequentative/intensive form of √dram ('to run, to go'). The frequentative conveys repeated, aimless, agitated motion — not walking, not even wandering, but staggering like a drunk or a dizzy person. Combined with pariyanti ('go round and round'), the image is of people moving energetically but in circles, never arriving anywhere. This is the Upanishad's verdict on the worldly life: it is not stillness but frenetic, purposeless activity. The modern analogy is unmistakable — busyness without direction, productivity without purpose, careers that go in circles. The deluded are not lazy; they are hyperactive. Their very activity is the symptom of their confusion.

sk: न साम्परायः प्रतिभाति बालं प्रमाद्यन्तं वित्तमोहेन मूढम् | अयं लोको नास्ति पर इति मानी पुनः पुनर्वशमापद्यते मे ||
ro: na · sāmparāyaḥ · pratibhāti · bālaṁ · pramādyantaṁ · vittamohena · mūḍham | ayaṁ · lokaḥ · na · asti · paraḥ · iti · mānī · punaḥ · punaḥ · vaśam · āpadyate · me ||
hi: धन के मोह से प्रमत्त और मूढ़ बने हुए बालक (अज्ञानी) को परलोक की बात सूझती ही नहीं। 'यही लोक है, परलोक कुछ नहीं' — ऐसा मानने वाला बार-बार मेरे (मृत्यु के) वश में आता है।
en: The hereafter never reveals itself to the childish one, who is heedless, deluded by the glamour of wealth. Thinking 'This world alone exists, there is no other' — such a one falls again and again under my sway.

ws.h: परलोक, मृत्यु के पश्चात् का लोक
ws.e: the hereafter, the world beyond — from sam+para+√i; what comes after this life
reveals itself, becomes apparent — prati+√bhā ('to shine forth'); the truth must shine upon the seeker
the childish one — not a child by age but by spiritual immaturity
heedless, careless — from pra+√mad ('to be intoxicated'); drunk on worldly life
by the delusion of wealth — vitta (wealth) + moha (delusion)

ws.h: मेरे वश में आ जाता है
ws.e: falls under my power — Yama speaks as Death personified; the materialist returns to death repeatedly

gr: bālam — 'childish one': not young in years but young in understanding; an adult who has never matured spiritually. pramādyantam — from pra+√mad: literally 'intoxicated'; the person is drunk on the world, heedless like one in a stupor. punaḥ punaḥ vaśam āpadyate me — 'again and again falls under MY power': Yama, the speaker, is Death himself. This is not a theological statement but a first-person testimony from Death: 'I catch such people repeatedly.' The cyclical nature of death-and-rebirth (punarjanma) is implied.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.6 — Yama speaks as Death in the first person — a unique rhetorical move. The one who denies the hereafter ('ayaṁ loko nāsti paraḥ') falls into death's power 'again and again' — a clear reference to the cycle of rebirth. The materialist's denial does not eliminate death but guarantees its repetition.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'पुनः पुनः' शब्द जन्म-मरण के चक्र (संसार) को इंगित करता है। जो आत्मा को नहीं जानता वह बार-बार मृत्यु के अधीन होता है। मृत्यु का अतिक्रमण केवल आत्मज्ञान से सम्भव है।
advaita.en: Shankara reads 'punaḥ punaḥ' as indicating the cycle of birth and death (saṁsāra). One who does not know the Self repeatedly falls under death's power. Transcendence of death is possible only through Self-knowledge.
advaita.ins: Death is not a one-time event but a recurring condition for the ignorant. Only the knowledge 'I am the deathless Atman' breaks the cycle.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि 'नास्ति परः' (कोई परलोक नहीं) — यह सबसे भयंकर अविद्या है। भगवान् ने जीवात्मा को शाश्वत बनाया है; उसे नश्वर मानना भगवान् का अपमान है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'nāsti paraḥ' (there is no beyond) is the most terrible form of ignorance. The Lord created the jīvātman as eternal; to consider it mortal is an insult to the Lord.
vishisht.ins: Materialism is not a philosophical position but a spiritual disease — it denies the very nature of the soul as the Lord created it.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'वित्तमोह' को भौतिक चेतना की सम्मोहन-शक्ति मानते हैं — पदार्थ का आकर्षण इतना प्रबल है कि चेतना उससे परे कुछ देख ही नहीं पाती। यही अविद्या का गहनतम रूप है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads 'vittamoha' as the hypnotic power of material consciousness — the attraction of matter is so strong that consciousness cannot see beyond it. This is the deepest form of ignorance.
aurobindo.ins: Matter itself is not the problem — it is consciousness imprisoned in matter that creates the illusion that nothing else exists.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Yama speak in the first person ('my power')?
dp.a: The phrase 'vaśam āpadyate me' — 'falls under MY power' — is remarkable because the speaker is Yama, the Lord of Death himself. This is not a theologian theorising about death; this is Death speaking from direct experience: 'I personally catch such people, again and again.' The first-person testimony makes the warning visceral and irrefutable — who knows death better than Death? The rhetorical effect is devastating: the materialist who says 'there is nothing beyond' is being directly contradicted by the one being beyond all others who would know. Yama has just spent Valli 1 testing Nachiketa with worldly temptations; now he reveals why those temptations exist — they are the bait that keeps people returning to his domain. Nachiketa's refusal was not merely admirable but existentially decisive.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'punaḥ punaḥ' (again and again) imply about the Upanishadic view of death?
dp.a: The phrase punaḥ punaḥ ('again and again') introduces the concept of punarjanma (rebirth) — or more precisely, punarmṛtyu (re-death). Death is not a single event but a recurring fate for those who lack Self-knowledge. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upanishad (1.2.7, 1.5.2) develops this concept explicitly: the ignorant person is subject to 'repeated death' (punarmṛtyu). In the Vedic period, this was considered even more terrifying than a single death — one might escape death once, but to face it again and again was the ultimate horror. The Katha Upanishad's solution — knowledge of the deathless Atman — is thus not merely philosophical but addresses the deepest existential anxiety of its time. Liberation (mokṣa) is, at its most basic level, the cessation of re-death.

sk: श्रवणायापि बहुभिर्यो न लभ्यः शृण्वन्तोऽपि बहवो यं न विद्युः | आश्चर्यो वक्ता कुशलोऽस्य लब्धाऽऽश्चर्यो ज्ञाता कुशलानुशिष्टः ||
ro: śravaṇāya · api · bahubhiḥ · yaḥ · na · labhyaḥ · śṛṇvanto · api · bahavo · yaṁ · na · vidyuḥ | āścaryo · vaktā · kuśalo · asya · labdhā · āścaryo · jñātā · kuśalānuśiṣṭaḥ ||
hi: जिसे (आत्मा को) बहुत लोगों को सुनने को भी नहीं मिलता; सुनकर भी बहुत लोग जिसे नहीं जान पाते; इसका वक्ता आश्चर्य है, इसका कुशल प्राप्तकर्ता आश्चर्य है, और कुशल गुरु द्वारा सिखाया गया ज्ञाता भी आश्चर्य है।
en: That (Self) which many do not even get to hear about, which many — even hearing — do not understand: wonderful is the teacher of it, skilful is the one who attains it, and wonderful is the knower who is instructed by a skilful teacher.

ws.e: even for hearing — dative of purpose; most people never even encounter the teaching
obtainable — gerundive of √labh; not easily available
would know — optative of √vid; even after hearing, understanding is not guaranteed
wonderful, a marvel — not 'surprising' but genuinely rare and wondrous
skilful, adept — not merely knowledgeable but practically accomplished
instructed by a skilled teacher — kuśala (skilled) + anuśiṣṭa (taught); the right teacher is essential

gr: śravaṇāya api na labhyaḥ — 'not even available for hearing': the rarity is layered — first, most never encounter the teaching; of those who hear, most don't understand; of those who understand intellectually, few truly know. āścaryaḥ — repeated twice to frame both teacher and knower as 'marvels.' kuśalānuśiṣṭaḥ — 'taught by a skilled one': the compound insists that even a qualified student needs the right guru.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.7 — This verse is echoed almost verbatim in the Bhagavad Gita (2.29). It establishes the extreme rarity of Self-knowledge — rare to hear, rarer to understand, rarest to realise. The three stages (hearing, understanding, realising) correspond to the Vedantic method of śravaṇa, manana, nididhyāsana.

advaita.h: शंकर इसमें आत्मज्ञान की दुर्लभता के तीन स्तर देखते हैं: (1) श्रवण — सुनने का अवसर, (2) मनन — सुनकर समझना, (3) निदिध्यासन — समझकर साक्षात्कार करना। प्रत्येक स्तर पर साधक कम होते जाते हैं।
advaita.en: Shankara sees three levels of rarity: (1) śravaṇa — the opportunity to hear, (2) manana — understanding after hearing, (3) nididhyāsana — realisation after understanding. At each level, seekers become fewer.
advaita.ins: Self-knowledge is like a filter with increasingly fine mesh — many approach, few pass through each stage, and the rarest is direct realisation.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि 'आश्चर्यः वक्ता' — सच्चा गुरु स्वयं एक चमत्कार है क्योंकि वह भगवान् की कृपा का माध्यम है। भगवान् स्वयं गुरु के रूप में प्रकट होते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'āścaryaḥ vaktā' — the true teacher is himself a miracle because he is the medium of the Lord's grace. The Lord manifests as the guru.
vishisht.ins: The guru is not just a human instructor but the Lord's compassion taking visible form. Finding such a teacher is itself the fruit of past merit.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि आत्मा का ज्ञान इसलिए दुर्लभ है क्योंकि यह मानसिक (mental) ज्ञान नहीं है — यह चेतना का रूपान्तरण है। सुनना बुद्धि से होता है, जानना अस्तित्व की गहराई से।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says Self-knowledge is rare because it is not mental knowledge — it is a transformation of consciousness. Hearing happens through the intellect; knowing happens from the depth of being.
aurobindo.ins: You cannot 'learn' the Self as you learn history or science. Knowing the Self means becoming the Self — a shift in being, not an acquisition of information.

dp.q: 🔍 How does this verse appear in the Bhagavad Gita?
dp.a: This verse is echoed almost word-for-word in the Bhagavad Gita 2.29: 'āścaryavat paśyati kaścid enam, āścaryavad vadati tathaiva cānyaḥ, āścaryavac cainam anyaḥ śṛṇoti, śrutvāpy enaṁ veda na caiva kaścit' — 'One sees it as a wonder; another speaks of it as a wonder; another hears of it as a wonder; and even after hearing, none knows it.' Krishna is drawing directly on Yama's teaching. The Gita context (Arjuna's grief over killing his kinsmen) is different, but the teaching is the same: the Atman is so subtle that ordinary cognition cannot grasp it. Both texts use the same cascade: even hearing about it is rare → understanding is rarer → direct knowing is rarest of all.

dp.q: 🔍 What do the three stages (hearing, understanding, knowing) correspond to in Vedantic practice?
dp.a: The three stages map precisely onto the triple method of Vedantic knowledge: Śravaṇa (hearing) — receiving the teaching from a qualified guru. Most people never even encounter a genuine teacher. Manana (reflection) — reasoning about what was heard, resolving doubts, integrating the teaching intellectually. Many hear but do not reflect deeply enough. Nididhyāsana (contemplation/meditation) — sustained, absorbed meditation on the truth until it becomes direct experience, not just intellectual understanding. This is the rarest stage. The verse's structure mirrors this exactly: 'many do not get to hear' (śravaṇa is rare), 'hearing, many do not understand' (manana fails), and the 'knower instructed by a skilled teacher' (nididhyāsana succeeds only with proper guidance). The method remains the standard Advaitic practice to this day.

sk: न नरेणावरेण प्रोक्त एष सुविज्ञेयो बहुधा चिन्त्यमानः | अनन्यप्रोक्ते गतिरत्र नास्ति अणीयान् ह्यतर्क्यमणुप्रमाणात् ||
ro: na · nareṇa · avareṇa · prokta · eṣa · suvijñeyo · bahudhā · cintyamānaḥ | ananyaprokте · gatiḥ · atra · na · asti · aṇīyān · hi · atarkyam · aṇupramāṇāt ||
hi: यह (आत्मा) किसी हीन (अयोग्य) मनुष्य द्वारा कहा जाने पर सुगमता से नहीं जाना जा सकता, और बहुत प्रकार से चिन्तन करने पर भी नहीं। जब तक कोई अन्य (श्रेष्ठ गुरु) न बताये, तब तक इसमें कोई गति नहीं — क्योंकि यह अणु से भी सूक्ष्म है, तर्क से अगम्य है।
en: This Self, when taught by an inferior person, cannot be easily understood, even when reflected upon in many ways. Unless taught by one who is one with it (ananya), there is no way to it — for it is subtler than the subtle, beyond the reach of reasoning.

ws.e: inferior, unqualified — one who has not realised the Self
easily knowable — su+vijñeya; even with many approaches, it is not 'easily known' from a wrong teacher

ws.h: बहुत प्रकार से चिन्तन किया गया
ws.e: reflected upon in many ways — bahudhā (variously) + cintyamāna (being thought about)
when taught by one who is non-different — an+anya+prokta; a teacher who IS the Self, not merely knows about it
subtler than the subtle — comparative of aṇu; finer than the finest atom
beyond reasoning — a+tarkya; logic cannot reach it

gr: avareṇa nareṇa — 'by an inferior man': not socially inferior but spiritually unqualified — one who has not realised the Self. ananyaprokte — this is the key compound: an+anya = 'not-other,' i.e., one who is non-different from the Self. Shankara reads this as a teacher who has directly realised Brahman. aṇīyān aṇupramāṇāt — 'subtler than the atomic measure': the Self is finer than the finest conceivable particle. atarkyam — 'beyond reasoning': tarka (logic) cannot reach it because the Self is the very ground from which tarka operates.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.8 — This verse establishes two critical principles: (1) the guru must be a realised soul (ananya), not merely learned; (2) the Self cannot be reached by logic alone (atarkyam). This verse is frequently cited in debates about the role of reasoning vs. revelation in Vedanta.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'अनन्यप्रोक्ते' का अर्थ है — जब ब्रह्मवित् (ब्रह्म को जानने वाला) गुरु बताये, तभी गति (मार्ग) है। 'अतर्क्यम्' — शुष्क तर्क से आत्मा नहीं जानी जा सकती; शास्त्र-प्रमाण और गुरु-कृपा आवश्यक है।
advaita.en: Shankara reads 'ananyaprokte' as: only when a Brahma-vid (knower of Brahman) teaches, is there a path. 'Atarkyam' — the Self cannot be known by dry reasoning alone; scriptural authority and guru's grace are necessary.
advaita.ins: Reasoning alone spins in circles because the mind cannot objectify its own source. The guru who IS the truth can point to what logic cannot reach.

vishisht.h: रामानुज 'अनन्य' में भगवत्-प्राप्त गुरु को देखते हैं — जो भगवान् से अभिन्न है। ऐसा गुरु भगवान् का ही प्रतिनिधि है। 'अतर्क्यम्' — भगवान् तर्क से परे हैं; केवल शरणागति से ही ज्ञात होते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja sees 'ananya' as a God-realised guru — one who is non-different from the Lord. Such a guru is the Lord's own representative. 'Atarkyam' — the Lord is beyond logic; He is known only through surrender.
vishisht.ins: The Self is not an object to be figured out but a reality to be surrendered to. The guru's role is to make this surrender possible.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'अतर्क्यम्' को बुद्धि की सीमा के रूप में पढ़ते हैं — तर्क (reason) मन (mind) का उपकरण है, और आत्मा मन से परे है। आत्मा को जानने के लिए मन को अतिक्रमण करना होगा — यही योग है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads 'atarkyam' as the limit of reason — tarka (logic) is an instrument of the mind, and the Self is beyond the mind. To know the Self, one must transcend the mind — this is the purpose of yoga.
aurobindo.ins: The mind is a magnificent instrument but it cannot know its own creator. To see the sun, you must use the sun's own light — to know the Self, you must become the Self.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'ananya' (non-different) mean for the guru-student relationship?
dp.a: The term ananya (an+anya = 'not-other') applied to the guru has profound implications. It means the qualified teacher is not different from the Self being taught. This is not a metaphor — in Advaita Vedanta, it means the guru has directly realised 'I am Brahman' and therefore speaks not about the Self but as the Self. The teaching is not information transfer but a transmission of being. This is why the Upanishads insist that books alone cannot liberate — the living presence of a realised teacher is essential because the teacher's very being demonstrates what words can only point to. The Chāndogya Upanishad (6.14.2) uses the analogy of a blindfolded person who needs someone to remove the blindfold and point the way — the text can describe the direction, but only the guru can remove the blindfold.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is the Self 'beyond reasoning' (atarkyam)?
dp.a: The Self is atarkyam (beyond reasoning) not because it is irrational but because reasoning operates within the field of the known while the Self is the knower itself. Consider: every act of reasoning requires a thinker who thinks, an observer who observes the thoughts. Reasoning can analyse everything that appears before consciousness, but it cannot turn around and grasp the consciousness in which it appears — just as the eye cannot see itself, or fire cannot burn itself. This is not a failure of logic but a structural impossibility. The Self is the ultimate subject that can never become an object of thought. This is why the Upanishads use a different method: neti neti ('not this, not this') — stripping away everything that is NOT the Self until only the Self remains, not as a conclusion but as the residual awareness that was present all along.

sk: नैषा तर्केण मतिरापनेया प्रोक्तान्येनैव सुज्ञानाय प्रेष्ठ | यां त्वमापः सत्यधृतिर्बतासि त्वादृङ्नो भूयान्नचिकेतः प्रष्टा ||
ro: na · eṣā · tarkeṇa · matiḥ · āpaneyā · proktā · anyena · eva · sujñānāya · preṣṭha | yāṁ · tvam · āpaḥ · satyadhṛtiḥ · bata · asi · tvādṛṅ · naḥ · bhūyāt · naciketaḥ · praṣṭā ||
hi: हे प्रिय! यह बुद्धि (आत्मज्ञान) तर्क से प्राप्त नहीं हो सकती; (किन्तु) किसी अन्य (सद्गुरु) द्वारा कही जाने पर यह सुगमता से जानी जा सकती है। तूने इसे प्राप्त कर लिया — तू सत्य में स्थिर है। हे नचिकेता! तेरे जैसा प्रश्नकर्ता हमें सदा मिले!
en: This understanding cannot be reached by reasoning alone. When taught by another (a true teacher), it is easily known, O dearest one. You have attained it — you are truly steadfast in truth. May we always find a questioner like you, O Nachiketa!

ws.e: by reasoning — instrumental of tarka; logic alone is insufficient
understanding, insight — not information but transformative insight
attainable — gerundive of ā+√āp ('to reach')
dearest — superlative of priya; Yama's deep affection for his student
steadfast in truth — satya (truth) + dhṛti (firmness); one whose resolve is rooted in truth
questioner — from √pracch ('to ask'); one who asks the right questions

gr: tarkeṇa na āpaneyā — 'cannot be attained by reasoning': continues the theme of atarkyam from verse 8. proktā anyena eva — 'when taught by another': the word 'anyena' here means a teacher who is 'other' than the student — i.e., a qualified guru (contrasting with the student's own reasoning). preṣṭha — superlative of priya: 'dearest one'; Yama's emotional regard for Nachiketa is palpable. satyadhṛtiḥ — 'truth-steadfast': the compound sums up Nachiketa's character in one word. tvādṛṅ naḥ bhūyāt praṣṭā — 'may we find a questioner like you': Yama, the greatest of teachers, praises his student — the ideal guru-śiṣya relationship is mutual.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.9 — Yama's affectionate exclamation 'preṣṭha' (dearest) and his wish for more students like Nachiketa reveals the emotional depth of the guru-student bond. The verse also restates the epistemological principle: reason alone fails; a qualified teacher is essential.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'तर्केण न आपनेया' — तर्क अनिश्चित है, एक तार्किक की बात दूसरा तार्किक काट देता है। आत्मज्ञान केवल शास्त्र और सद्गुरु के उपदेश से सम्भव है। नचिकेता 'सत्यधृतिः' है — सत्य में उसकी धृति (दृढ़ता) ने उसे योग्य बनाया।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'tarkeṇa na āpaneyā' — reasoning is inconclusive; one logician's argument is refuted by another. Self-knowledge is possible only through scripture and a true teacher's instruction. Nachiketa is 'satyadhṛtiḥ' — his firmness in truth made him worthy.
advaita.ins: Philosophy without revelation runs in circles. The guru and the scripture together provide the compass that reasoning alone cannot.

vishisht.h: रामानुज 'प्रेष्ठ' शब्द में गुरु-शिष्य के प्रेम-सम्बन्ध को देखते हैं। भगवान् भी अपने भक्त को 'प्रिय' कहते हैं (गीता 18.65)। यम नचिकेता से वैसा ही स्नेह रखते हैं — यह दैवी प्रेम है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja sees in 'preṣṭha' the love-bond between guru and disciple. The Lord also calls His devotee 'priya' (Gita 18.65). Yama feels the same affection for Nachiketa — this is divine love.
vishisht.ins: The guru-student relationship is not merely academic but deeply personal — it mirrors the Lord's love for the devoted soul.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'त्वादृङ् नो भूयात् प्रष्टा' में आदर्श साधक की दुर्लभता देखते हैं। सही प्रश्न पूछना सही उत्तर पाने से भी कठिन है — नचिकेता का प्रश्न ('मृत्यु के बाद क्या है?') ही उसकी सर्वोच्च योग्यता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees in 'tvādṛṅ naḥ bhūyāt praṣṭā' the rarity of the ideal seeker. Asking the right question is harder than finding the right answer — Nachiketa's question ('What is beyond death?') is itself his supreme qualification.
aurobindo.ins: The quality of the question determines the quality of the answer. Nachiketa's question was total — he was willing to die for it — and so the answer he received was total.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Yama call Nachiketa 'preṣṭha' (dearest)?
dp.a: Yama's use of preṣṭha (superlative of priya — 'the most dear') is profoundly significant. This is Death himself — the most feared being in existence — expressing deep affection for a student. The word reveals that the guru-śiṣya relationship, when authentic, transcends even the boundary between life and death. Yama has tested Nachiketa with his most powerful temptations and the boy has passed every test. This creates a bond of mutual respect: the student proved worthy by refusing everything; the teacher honours that worthiness with the highest term of endearment. In the broader Hindu tradition, the guru-student bond is considered greater than the parent-child bond because it concerns the birth of the soul, not merely the body. Yama, who has no biological children (he is Death), finds in Nachiketa a spiritual son.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'satyadhṛtiḥ' (steadfast in truth) reveal about Nachiketa's character?
dp.a: Satyadhṛtiḥ is a compound of satya (truth) and dhṛti (firmness, resolve, steadfastness). It is the single word that captures Nachiketa's entire character arc. In Valli 1, we saw Nachiketa's dhṛti in action — he waited three nights at Death's door without food; he rejected wealth, longevity, beautiful women, and kingdoms. But this firmness was not mere stubbornness — it was rooted in satya, in truth. He refused the pleasant because he could see it was not the true. This combination — firmness that is truth-rooted, not ego-driven — is what makes Nachiketa the ideal student. The Gita will later define dhṛti in three grades (18.33-35): sāttvic dhṛti holds fast to yoga and truth; rājasic dhṛti holds fast to duty and pleasure; tāmasic dhṛti clings to sleep and fear. Nachiketa's is purely sāttvic — he holds fast to nothing except truth itself.

sk: जानाम्यहं शेवधिरित्यनित्यं न ह्यध्रुवैः प्राप्यते हि ध्रुवं तत् | ततो मया नाचिकेतश्चितोऽग्निरनित्यैर्द्रव्यैः प्रतिपादितवानस्मि नित्यम् ||
ro: jānāmi · ahaṁ · śevadhiḥ · iti · anityaṁ · na · hi · adhruvaiḥ · prāpyate · hi · dhruvaṁ · tat | tato · mayā · nāciketaḥ · citaḥ · agniḥ · anityaiḥ · dravyaiḥ · pratipāditavān · asmi · nityam ||
hi: मैं (यम) जानता हूँ कि शेवधि (सांसारिक निधि) अनित्य है। अनित्य वस्तुओं से उस नित्य (शाश्वत तत्त्व) की प्राप्ति नहीं होती। फिर भी मैंने अनित्य द्रव्यों से नाचिकेत अग्नि का चयन किया — और उन अनित्य द्रव्यों से मैंने नित्य को प्राप्त किया है।
en: I know that the treasure (of worldly things) is transient. The Eternal cannot be attained by the non-eternal. Yet I have built the Nachiketa fire with transient materials — and through those transient means I have attained the Eternal.

ws.e: treasure, store of wealth — the accumulated possessions of worldly life
impermanent, transient — an+nitya; all worldly goods are temporary
by the non-eternal, by unstable things — a+dhruva (not firm)
the eternal, the stable — dhruva means 'fixed, permanent'
built, arranged — past participle of √ci ('to pile up, build'); the fire-altar is constructed
I have attained — perfect active periphrastic; Yama confirms his own realisation

gr: śevadhiḥ iti anityam — 'the treasure is impermanent': Yama knows from direct experience that all worldly possessions are fleeting. na adhruvaiḥ prāpyate dhruvam — 'the permanent is not attained by the impermanent': this states the fundamental impossibility — yet the next line paradoxically claims Yama did exactly that. anityaiḥ dravyaiḥ nityam pratipāditavān — 'by impermanent materials I attained the permanent': the paradox is resolved by understanding that the fire-ritual, though using material things, serves as a vehicle for transcendence.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.10 — This verse presents a crucial paradox: the eternal cannot be reached through the non-eternal, yet Yama built the Nachiketa fire with non-eternal materials and attained the eternal. The resolution: the fire-ritual is a bridge between worlds — material in form but spiritual in function.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यम स्वयं इस विरोधाभास को स्वीकार करते हैं — अनित्य से नित्य नहीं मिलता, फिर भी कर्म (अग्नि-चयन) एक सोपान के रूप में काम करता है। किन्तु अन्ततः केवल ज्ञान ही मुक्ति देता है — कर्म केवल चित्त-शुद्धि करता है।
advaita.en: Shankara notes that Yama himself acknowledges the paradox — the non-eternal cannot yield the eternal, yet ritual action (fire-building) serves as a step. But ultimately, only knowledge liberates — action merely purifies the mind.
advaita.ins: Ritual is the ladder, not the destination. It purifies the mind enough to receive knowledge, but it is knowledge alone that liberates.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् की कृपा से अनित्य साधन भी नित्य फल दे सकते हैं। नाचिकेत अग्नि भगवान् की पूजा का साधन है — भगवान् की कृपा ही अनित्य को नित्य से जोड़ती है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says that through the Lord's grace, even impermanent means can yield eternal results. The Nachiketa fire is a means of worshipping the Lord — and it is the Lord's grace that bridges the transient and the eternal.
vishisht.ins: Human effort is transient; divine grace transforms it into something eternal. The devotee's offering, however small, becomes infinite through the Lord's acceptance.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द इस विरोधाभास में भौतिक और आध्यात्मिक का सम्बन्ध देखते हैं — पदार्थ (matter) अपने-आप में अनित्य है, किन्तु जब चेतना उसे रूपान्तरित करती है तो वह शाश्वत की अभिव्यक्ति बन जाता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees in this paradox the relationship between matter and spirit — matter is impermanent in itself, but when consciousness transforms it, matter becomes an expression of the eternal.
aurobindo.ins: The material world is not opposed to the spiritual — it is the unfinished expression of spirit. Through conscious action, the transient becomes the vehicle of the permanent.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the paradox of attaining the eternal through the non-eternal?
dp.a: This verse presents one of the deepest paradoxes in Indian philosophy. The principle is clear: na adhruvaiḥ prāpyate dhruvam — 'the permanent cannot be attained by the impermanent.' Bricks, wood, ghee, mantras spoken in time — all are non-eternal. How can they yield an eternal result? Shankara's resolution: the fire-ritual does not produce the eternal (Brahman is not a product) but purifies the mind so it can recognise what was always there. The fire is a mirror-polisher, not a mirror-maker. Ramanuja's resolution: the Lord's grace transforms the offering — the devotee's impermanent act is accepted by the permanent Lord, who grants eternal results. Aurobindo's resolution: matter and spirit are not truly separate — conscious action in matter is spirit expressing itself through matter. All three agree: the bridge is real, but the mechanism differs — purification, grace, or transformation.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the Nachiketa fire (nāciketāgni) and why does Yama mention it here?
dp.a: The Nachiketa fire (nāciketāgni) was taught by Yama in Valli 1 (mantras 14-16) as the second boon. It is a specific arrangement of the fire-altar — the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa describes it in detail. Yama mentions it here because it creates a contrast within his own experience: he knows perfectly well that worldly treasures are impermanent, yet he himself built a fire-altar from impermanent materials and attained something permanent through it. He is being intellectually honest — he states the principle ('the eternal cannot come from the non-eternal') and then admits his own apparent violation of it. This honesty makes the teaching more powerful: even the Lord of Death navigates this paradox. The resolution is that the fire-ritual works not by producing the eternal but by orienting the practitioner toward it — it is a practice of attention, surrender, and purification that makes the mind fit to receive what was always present.

sk: कामस्याप्तिं जगतः प्रतिष्ठां क्रतोरनन्त्यमभयस्य पारम् | स्तोममहदुरुगायं प्रतिष्ठां दृष्ट्वा धृत्या धीरो नचिकेतोऽत्यस्राक्षीः ||
ro: kāmasya · āptiṁ · jagataḥ · pratiṣṭhāṁ · kratoḥ · ānantyam · abhayasya · pāram | stomam · mahad · urugāyaṁ · pratiṣṭhāṁ · dṛṣṭvā · dhṛtyā · dhīro · naciketo · atyasrākṣīḥ ||
hi: कामनाओं की तृप्ति को, जगत् की प्रतिष्ठा (आधार) को, अनन्त कर्मफल को, निर्भयता के पार (शान्ति) को, महान् स्तोम (स्तुति) को, विस्तृत (उरुगाय) कीर्ति को — इन सबको देखकर भी, हे धीर नचिकेता, तूने धैर्यपूर्वक इन सबको त्याग दिया।
en: The fulfilment of desires, the foundation of the world, the endlessness of ritual merit, the far shore of fearlessness, the great praise, the wide renown — seeing all these, you, O wise Nachiketa, with firmness cast them aside.

ws.e: the fulfilment of desires — everything one could wish for
the foundation of the world — worldly eminence and establishment
endlessness of ritual merit — infinite results of sacrifice
the far shore of fearlessness — the ultimate refuge of safety
great praise — universal acclaim and glory

ws.h: विस्तृत कीर्ति वाला, दूर तक गाया जाने वाला
ws.e: widely sung, far-famed — uru (wide) + gāya (singing)
with firmness, with resolve — instrumental of dhṛti

gr: kāmasya āptim ... urugāyam pratiṣṭhām — this is a catalogue of everything the world values: desire-fulfilment, worldly eminence, infinite merit, fearlessness, praise, and fame. dṛṣṭvā dhṛtyā atyasrākṣīḥ — 'having seen, with firmness, cast aside': the same decisive verb (atyasrākṣīḥ) from verse 3. Nachiketa did not reject blindly — he saw (dṛṣṭvā) all the offerings clearly and then released them with deliberate firmness (dhṛtyā).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.11 — Yama recapitulates the temptation scene from Valli 1 in condensed form. This verse serves as a bridge — Yama is summing up why Nachiketa is qualified, before turning to the actual metaphysical teaching in the next verse.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यम यहाँ नचिकेता के वैराग्य की महिमा गा रहे हैं — जो व्यक्ति इन सब को देखकर भी त्याग सके, केवल वही आत्मज्ञान का अधिकारी है। यह वैराग्य सर्वोत्कृष्ट है।
advaita.en: Shankara says Yama is celebrating Nachiketa's vairāgya — only one who can see all these and still let go is fit for Self-knowledge. This is the highest form of dispassion.
advaita.ins: Dispassion is not deprivation but clarity — seeing the full magnificence of the world and still choosing what lies beyond it.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि नचिकेता ने जो कुछ त्यागा वह सब भगवान् की विभूतियाँ थीं — किन्तु विभूति से बड़ा विभूतिमान् (भगवान् स्वयं) है। नचिकेता ने भगवान् को चुना, उनकी विभूतियों को नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says everything Nachiketa rejected was a manifestation of the Lord's glory — but the Lord Himself is greater than all His glories. Nachiketa chose the Lord, not His manifestations.
vishisht.ins: The world's splendour is a reflection of the divine — but the wise seek the source of the reflection, not the reflection itself.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'दृष्ट्वा' (देखकर) शब्द पर बल देते हैं — नचिकेता ने सब कुछ देखा, अनुभव किया, और फिर उसके पार जाने का संकल्प किया। यह अज्ञान से नहीं, चेतना की उच्चतर दृष्टि से किया गया त्याग है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo emphasises 'dṛṣṭvā' (having seen) — Nachiketa saw everything, experienced it, and then resolved to go beyond. This is renunciation born not of ignorance but of the higher vision of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The truest renunciation comes after the fullest seeing. One must know what one is giving up — otherwise it is merely lack of opportunity, not genuine transcendence.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Yama list so many temptations in a single verse?
dp.a: The catalogue of temptations — desire-fulfilment, world-eminence, infinite merit, fearlessness, praise, fame — is deliberately overwhelming. Yama is making the point that Nachiketa did not merely reject one or two temptations but the entire spectrum of what the world can offer. Each item represents a different dimension of worldly value: kāmasya āpti (pleasure), jagataḥ pratiṣṭhā (status), kratoḥ ānantyam (religious merit), abhayasya pāram (security), stomam mahat (recognition), urugāyam (fame). Together they cover every motivational category: hedonistic, social, religious, existential, and reputational. Nachiketa refused them all. The comprehensiveness of the list proves the comprehensiveness of his vairāgya — there is no angle of temptation left untried.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'dhṛtyā' (with firmness) add to the picture?
dp.a: Dhṛtyā (instrumental of dhṛti) means 'with firmness, with steadfast resolve.' It is paired with dṛṣṭvā (having seen) to create a two-stage portrait: first sight, then resolve. Nachiketa did not flinch, panic, or hurry — he saw everything offered, understood its value, and then with deliberate firmness released it. This is not the renunciation of the overwhelmed or the indifferent but the renunciation of the clear-eyed. The Gita (18.33) defines sāttvic dhṛti as 'that by which one holds firm the activities of the mind, prāṇa, and senses through unwavering yoga.' Nachiketa embodies this: his dhṛti is not suppression of desire but the stable, unwavering commitment to truth that makes desire irrelevant. The word also contains a quiet contrast with the 'manda' of verse 2 — the manda lacks dhṛti and so collapses into preyas at the first pressure.

sk: तं दुर्दर्शं गूढमनुप्रविष्टं गुहाहितं गह्वरेष्ठं पुराणम् | अध्यात्मयोगाधिगमेन देवं मत्वा धीरो हर्षशोकौ जहाति ||
ro: taṁ · durdarśaṁ · gūḍham · anupraviṣṭaṁ · guhāhitaṁ · gahvareṣṭhaṁ · purāṇam | adhyātmayoga · adhigamena · devaṁ · matvā · dhīro · harṣaśokau · jahāti ||
hi: उस दुर्दर्श (कठिनाई से दिखने वाले), गूढ़ (छिपे हुए), गुहा में स्थित, गह्वर (गहराई) में बसे हुए, पुरातन देव (आत्मा) को — अध्यात्म-योग के माध्यम से जानकर — धीर पुरुष हर्ष और शोक दोनों को त्याग देता है।
en: That (Self) — hard to see, deeply hidden, entered into the cave (of the heart), dwelling in the abyss, the ancient one — having known this God through the yoga of the Self (adhyātma-yoga), the wise one leaves behind both joy and sorrow.

ws.e: hard to see — dur+darśa; not invisible but requiring extraordinary vision
hidden, concealed — past participle of √guh ('to hide')
entered into — anu+pra+√viś; the Self has entered into everything
placed in the cave — guhā (cave = the heart) + āhita (placed); the heart-cave is the Self's seat
dwelling in the depth — gahvara (abyss, depth) + stha (standing)
ancient, primeval — existing from before time began
by the attainment of adhyātma-yoga — the yoga directed toward the inner Self
joy and sorrow — the two poles of emotional experience; both transcended

gr: durdarśam gūḍham anupraviṣṭam guhāhitam gahvareṣṭham purāṇam — six adjectives piled one upon another, each deepening the description of the Self's hiddenness. guhāhitam — 'placed in the cave': the guhā is the heart (hṛdaya), the innermost chamber of being. adhyātmayoga — 'yoga directed at the Self': adhyātma (relating to the Self) + yoga (discipline, union). harṣaśokau jahāti — 'abandons joy and sorrow': the wise one goes beyond the duality of pleasure and pain.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.12 — This verse marks the transition from Yama's validation of Nachiketa to the actual metaphysical teaching. The six adjectives of the Self (durdarśa, gūḍha, anupraviṣṭa, guhāhita, gahvareṣṭha, purāṇa) form one of the richest descriptions of the Atman in the Upanishads. The phrase 'guhāhita' (dwelling in the heart-cave) becomes central to the Katha's teaching.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'गुहाहितम्' — आत्मा बुद्धि की गुहा (गुफा) में छिपा है। वह बाहर नहीं, भीतर है; इन्द्रियों से नहीं, अध्यात्म-योग से जाना जाता है। 'हर्षशोकौ जहाति' — आत्मज्ञानी द्वन्द्वों से परे होता है।
advaita.en: Shankara reads 'guhāhitam' — the Self is hidden in the cave of the intellect (buddhi). It is within, not outside; known not through the senses but through adhyātma-yoga. 'Harṣaśokau jahāti' — the knower of the Self transcends all dualities.
advaita.ins: The Self is the closest thing to us — closer than our own thoughts — yet it is the last thing we find because we always look outward.

vishisht.h: रामानुज 'देवम्' शब्द पर बल देते हैं — आत्मा केवल एक तत्त्व नहीं, यह 'देव' (दिव्य) है — भगवान् का अंश है। 'गुहाहितम्' — भगवान् प्रत्येक हृदय में अन्तर्यामी रूप में विराजमान हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja emphasises 'devam' — the Self is not merely a principle but 'deva' (divine) — a portion of the Lord. 'Guhāhitam' — the Lord dwells within every heart as the inner controller (antaryāmī).
vishisht.ins: The divine is not far away in some distant heaven but closer than your own heartbeat — dwelling in the very cave of your heart.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'अध्यात्मयोग' को आन्तरिक रूपान्तरण की प्रक्रिया मानते हैं — बाहरी साधना नहीं बल्कि चेतना की अन्तर्मुखी यात्रा। 'पुराणम्' — आत्मा समय से परे है, अनादि है; जो 'गह्वरेष्ठ' (गहराई में बसा) है वही सारी सृष्टि का मूल है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads 'adhyātmayoga' as the process of inner transformation — not external practice but the inward journey of consciousness. 'Purāṇam' — the Self is beyond time, beginningless; that which 'dwells in the depth' (gahvareṣṭha) is the source of all creation.
aurobindo.ins: The Self is both the most ancient and the most intimate reality — it was before time began and it is here, now, in the silent cave of the heart.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the 'cave of the heart' (guhā)?
dp.a: The guhā (cave) is one of the most important metaphors in the Upanishads. It refers to the hṛdaya (heart) — not the physical organ but the innermost chamber of consciousness, the subtle space within which the Self is 'placed' (āhita). The Chāndogya Upanishad (8.1.1) describes it: 'As vast as this outer space is the space within the heart. Within it are contained both heaven and earth, both fire and wind, both sun and moon.' The heart-cave is simultaneously the most intimate and the most vast — smaller than the smallest, larger than the largest (Katha 1.2.20). Meditation traditions across Hinduism direct attention to this inner space — the hṛdayākāśa (space of the heart) — as the seat of the Self. The metaphor of a cave adds the dimension of hiddenness: the Self is not displayed openly but must be sought in the depths, like a treasure in a cave.

dp.q: 🔍 What is adhyātma-yoga?
dp.a: Adhyātma-yoga is a compound of adhyātma (relating to the Self, the inner) and yoga (discipline, practice, union). It means the discipline directed inward toward the Self, as distinct from external ritual, social ethics, or devotional worship. In the Katha Upanishad's context, it encompasses the entire method of Self-knowledge: withdrawal of the senses from their objects, concentration of the mind, and direct contemplation of the Self in the heart-cave. Shankara interprets it as the threefold practice of śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana. The Gita (chapters 6 and 13) develops the concept further. What distinguishes adhyātma-yoga from other paths is its direction: it does not seek anything outside — no heaven, no deity, no merit — but turns consciousness back upon itself until the knower recognises that it IS the known. The 'adhigamena' (by attainment) specifies that this is not theory but realisation.

sk: एतच्छ्रुत्वा सम्परिगृह्य मर्त्यः प्रवृह्य धर्म्यमणुमेतमाप्य | स मोदते मोदनीयं हि लब्ध्वा विवृतं सद्म नचिकेतसं मन्ये ||
ro: etac · chrutvā · samparigṛhya · martyaḥ · pravṛhya · dharmyam · aṇum · etam · āpya | sa · modate · modanīyaṁ · hi · labdhvā · vivṛtaṁ · sadma · naciketasaṁ · manye ||
hi: इस (आत्मतत्त्व) को सुनकर, भली-भाँति ग्रहण करके, मर्त्य (मनुष्य) इस सूक्ष्म धर्म्य तत्त्व को पृथक् करके और प्राप्त करके, आनन्दित होता है — क्योंकि उसने आनन्द के योग्य तत्त्व को पा लिया है। मैं समझता हूँ कि नचिकेता के लिए (ज्ञान का) द्वार खुला है।
en: Having heard this, having fully grasped it, the mortal draws out this subtle essence of dharma and attains it — he rejoices, for he has obtained what is truly worthy of rejoicing. I consider the abode (of Brahman) to be open for Nachiketa.

ws.e: having fully grasped — sam+pari+√grah; thorough comprehension, not superficial hearing
having drawn out, extracted — pra+√vṛh; like extracting the essence from a plant
the subtle essence of dharma — the finest, most essential truth
rejoices — √mud; the joy of realisation, not sensory pleasure
worthy of rejoicing — gerundive of √mud; truly deserving of joy
the opened abode — vivṛta (opened) + sadma (dwelling); the gates of Brahman are open

gr: pravṛhya dharmyam aṇum — 'having drawn out the subtle dharma': the image is of extracting the finest essence, like drawing out a fibre from a stalk (or the famous muñja-grass image from 2.3.17). modate modanīyaṁ labdhvā — 'rejoices having obtained what is worth rejoicing': a beautiful figure of repetition (polyptoton) — the joy and its object are both expressed through the same root. vivṛtaṁ sadma — 'the opened abode': Brahman's door is open for the qualified seeker.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.13 — The image of 'drawing out the subtle essence' (pravṛhya dharmyam aṇum) anticipates the famous muñja-grass simile in 2.3.17. 'Vivṛtam sadma' — Yama declares the door to Brahman open for Nachiketa, formally beginning the esoteric teaching.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'प्रवृह्य' (पृथक् करके) का अर्थ है आत्मा को अनात्मा से अलग करना — जैसे ईख से रस निकाला जाता है। 'मोदते' — यह आनन्द सांसारिक सुख नहीं, ब्रह्मानन्द है।
advaita.en: Shankara reads 'pravṛhya' (drawing out) as separating the Self from the non-Self — like extracting juice from sugarcane. 'Modate' — this joy is not worldly happiness but the bliss of Brahman.
advaita.ins: Self-realisation is like extracting the innermost essence — what remains when every layer of not-Self is peeled away is pure bliss.

vishisht.h: रामानुज 'विवृतम् सद्म' — खुला हुआ निवास — में भगवान् के परमधाम का द्वार देखते हैं। भगवान् का धाम सदा है, किन्तु अधिकारी भक्त के लिए ही उसका द्वार खुलता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja reads 'vivṛtam sadma' — the opened abode — as the gate to the Lord's supreme dwelling (paramadhāma). The Lord's abode always exists, but its gate opens only for the qualified devotee.
vishisht.ins: The gate to the divine is not locked from the outside — it opens from within, when the seeker's heart is ready.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'मोदते' में आत्म-साक्षात्कार के आनन्द को देखते हैं — यह बाहर से नहीं आता, यह आत्मा का स्वभाव ही आनन्द है। 'विवृतम् सद्म' — चेतना का नया क्षेत्र खुल गया है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees in 'modate' the bliss of Self-realisation — it does not come from outside; bliss IS the nature of the Self. 'Vivṛtam sadma' — a new field of consciousness has opened up.
aurobindo.ins: Joy is not the reward of finding the Self — joy is what the Self IS. The seeker does not gain happiness; they discover they were happiness all along.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'drawing out the subtle dharma' mean practically?
dp.a: The phrase pravṛhya dharmyam aṇum ('having drawn out the subtle essence of dharma') uses the verb pravṛhya (from pra+√vṛh, 'to pull out, extract'). The image is of carefully extracting something extremely fine from within something coarse — like drawing a silk thread from a cocoon, or extracting the pith from a reed. Practically, this describes the process of discrimination (viveka): separating the eternal Self from the layers of non-Self that surround it (body, mind, ego, sensations, thoughts). The Self is already there, fully present — it does not need to be created or imported. It needs to be extracted from the mass of identification with what is not-Self. This is why the Upanishadic method is sometimes called 'neti neti' ('not this, not this') — each negation strips away a layer, until only the unconditioned Self remains. The extraction is not violent but precise — like a surgeon's scalpel, not a warrior's sword.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the 'opened abode' (vivṛtam sadma)?
dp.a: Yama declares vivṛtaṁ sadma naciketasaṁ manye — 'I consider the abode to be open for Nachiketa.' The sadma (abode, dwelling) refers to Brahman — the ultimate reality, the 'home' of the Self. The word vivṛtam (opened) implies that this abode was previously closed — not because Brahman was ever inaccessible in principle, but because the seeker was not ready. Now that Nachiketa has passed every test — ethical (rejecting temptations), intellectual (distinguishing śreyas from preyas), and existential (choosing death-knowledge over life-pleasures) — the door is open. This is a formal declaration of initiation: Yama is saying, in effect, 'You are ready. What I am about to teach you is not locked away — it is open to you.' The metaphor resonates across traditions: the 'narrow gate' of the Gospels, the 'gateless gate' of Zen — the barrier was never in the teaching but in the seeker's readiness.

sk: अन्यत्र धर्मादन्यत्राधर्मादन्यत्रास्मात्कृताकृतात् | अन्यत्र भूताच्च भव्याच्च यत्तत्पश्यसि तद्वद ||
ro: anyatra · dharmād · anyatra · adharmād · anyatra · asmāt · kṛtākṛtāt | anyatra · bhūtāc · ca · bhavyāc · ca · yat · tat · paśyasi · tad · vada ||
hi: नचिकेता ने कहा — जो धर्म से भिन्न है, अधर्म से भिन्न है, इस कार्य-कारण (कृत-अकृत) से भिन्न है, भूत (अतीत) और भव्य (भविष्य) दोनों से भिन्न है — जो उस (तत्त्व) को आप देखते हैं, वह बताइये।
en: Nachiketa said: That which is beyond dharma and adharma, beyond cause and effect, beyond past and future — that which you see, tell me that.

ws.e: beyond, other than — repeated four times for emphasis; the Self is beyond every category
beyond dharma — even righteous action cannot define the Self
beyond adharma — nor is it defined by its opposite

ws.h: किये हुए और न किये हुए से, कार्य-कारण से
ws.e: beyond the done and undone — kṛta (done) + akṛta (undone); beyond the entire domain of action
beyond the past — bhūta (what has been)
beyond the future — bhavya (what is to be)

gr: anyatra — repeated four times: 'beyond dharma, beyond adharma, beyond cause-and-effect, beyond past-and-future.' Each repetition strips away another category of thought. kṛtākṛtāt — 'beyond the done and the undone': this transcends the entire domain of karma and action. bhūtāc ca bhavyāc ca — 'beyond past and future': the Self is beyond time itself. yat tat paśyasi tad vada — 'that which you see, tell me that': Nachiketa asks not for theory but for Yama's direct vision.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.14 — Nachiketa's question is perfectly formulated: he asks for that which transcends all dualities — dharma/adharma, cause/effect, past/future. This is the quintessential Upanishadic question: what is the unconditioned reality beyond all categories?

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि नचिकेता का प्रश्न ही उसकी योग्यता है — उसने सीधे ब्रह्म को माँगा: धर्म-अधर्म से परे, कार्य-कारण से परे, काल से परे। यही निर्गुण ब्रह्म की परिभाषा है।
advaita.en: Shankara says Nachiketa's question itself demonstrates his fitness — he asked directly for Brahman: beyond dharma-adharma, beyond cause-effect, beyond time. This is the very definition of Nirguṇa Brahman.
advaita.ins: The right question already contains the answer. By asking for that which is beyond all categories, Nachiketa shows he already intuits the unconditioned.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि 'अन्यत्र धर्मात्' का अर्थ है कि भगवान् धर्म-अधर्म से परे हैं — वे सम्पूर्ण नैतिक व्यवस्था के स्रोत हैं, उसके अधीन नहीं। भगवान् काल से भी परे हैं — काल उनकी सृष्टि है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'anyatra dharmāt' means the Lord is beyond dharma-adharma — He is the source of the entire moral order, not subject to it. The Lord is also beyond time — time is His creation.
vishisht.ins: God is not bound by the rules He creates. Dharma governs creation; the Creator transcends dharma.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द इसमें चेतना के सर्वोच्च स्तर की खोज देखते हैं — जो सभी द्वन्द्वों (dharma/adharma), सभी प्रक्रियाओं (kṛta/akṛta), और काल (bhūta/bhavya) से परे है। यही सच्चिदानन्द (sat-cit-ānanda) है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees here the search for the highest level of consciousness — beyond all dualities (dharma/adharma), all processes (kṛta/akṛta), and time itself (bhūta/bhavya). This is Saccidānanda (existence-consciousness-bliss).
aurobindo.ins: The ultimate reality is not a bigger version of what we know — it transcends every category of knowing. The mind must let go of all its frameworks to approach it.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Nachiketa ask for something 'beyond dharma'?
dp.a: Nachiketa's request for that which is anyatra dharmāt (beyond dharma) is startling because dharma is the highest principle in the Vedic worldview — it is the cosmic law, the moral order, the foundation of civilisation. To ask for something beyond dharma is to ask for the unconditioned absolute — that which cannot be captured by any human category, even the most exalted. This is not a rejection of dharma but a recognition of its limitation: dharma governs the phenomenal world, but the Self is not a phenomenon. Dharma tells you what to do; the Self is the one who does. Dharma is a rule; the Self is the reality that makes rules possible. By framing his question this way, Nachiketa demonstrates that he is not seeking ethical guidance or religious instruction but the ground of being itself.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'beyond past and future' (anyatra bhūtāc ca bhavyāc ca) mean for the Self?
dp.a: To be beyond past and future means to be beyond time. This is one of the most radical Upanishadic claims: the Self is not in time. It is not something that was born in the past and will die in the future; it is not a process that unfolds through time; it is not even an eternal being that endures through time. It is beyond time — it is the timeless ground in which time appears. The Māṇḍūkya Upanishad (verse 7) makes this explicit in its description of Turīya (the fourth state): it is 'not past, not future, not present.' The Self is the eternal Now — not a moment in the flow of time but the awareness in which time flows. Past and future are categories of the mind; the Self is the witness of the mind. This is why Self-knowledge is not a memory (of the past) or a hope (for the future) but a direct recognition in the present.

sk: सर्वे वेदा यत्पदमामनन्ति तपांसि सर्वाणि च यद्वदन्ति | यदिच्छन्तो ब्रह्मचर्यं चरन्ति तत्ते पदं सङ्ग्रहेण ब्रवीम्योमित्येतत् ||
ro: sarve · vedā · yat · padam · āmananti · tapāṁsi · sarvāṇi · ca · yad · vadanti | yad · icchanto · brahmacaryaṁ · caranti · tat · te · padaṁ · saṅgraheṇa · bravīmi · om · iti · etat ||
hi: सब वेद जिस पद (लक्ष्य) को कहते हैं, सब तपस्याएँ जिसकी बात करती हैं, जिसे चाहते हुए लोग ब्रह्मचर्य का पालन करते हैं — उस पद को मैं तुझे संक्षेप में बताता हूँ — वह ॐ है।
en: That goal which all the Vedas declare, which all austerities proclaim, and desiring which people practise brahmacharya — that goal I tell you briefly: it is OM.

ws.e: goal, destination, state — literally 'step' or 'place'; the ultimate destination of all seeking
declare, transmit — ā+√man; the Vedas unanimously point to this
austerities, penances — all forms of tapas (spiritual heat/discipline)
celibacy / the life of a student devoted to Brahman — brahma (Brahman) + carya (conduct)
in brief, in summary — sam+graha; condensing the entire teaching into one syllable
OM — the sacred syllable; the sonic symbol of Brahman

gr: sarve vedā yat padam āmananti — 'all the Vedas declare this goal': the unanimity is stressed — not one Veda but all of them converge on this single point. saṅgraheṇa bravīmi — 'I tell you in brief': Yama distils the entire Vedic corpus into one syllable. om iti etat — 'it is OM': the answer is breathtaking in its simplicity — after verses of complex description, the destination is a single sound.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.15 — This is one of the most celebrated verses in the Upanishads, directly quoted in the Bhagavad Gita (8.13). OM is presented as the sonic embodiment of Brahman — the single syllable that contains the entire Veda. The Mandukya Upanishad is entirely devoted to unpacking this syllable.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि ॐ ब्रह्म का प्रतीक (symbol) और ब्रह्म स्वयं — दोनों है। जैसे राजा का नाम राजा को इंगित करता है, वैसे ही ॐ ब्रह्म को। ॐ का उच्चारण चित्त को ब्रह्म की ओर मोड़ता है।
