advaita.en: Shankara says OM is both the symbol of Brahman and Brahman itself — just as a king's name points to the king, OM points to Brahman. The utterance of OM turns the mind toward Brahman.
advaita.ins: OM is not an arbitrary label but the natural sonic expression of ultimate reality — the sound that consciousness makes when it recognises itself.

vishisht.h: रामानुज ॐ को भगवान् के नाम के रूप में देखते हैं — यह भगवान् का सर्वप्रथम और सर्वोच्च नाम है। ॐ का जप भगवान् की पूजा है, भगवान् के ध्यान का सर्वोत्तम साधन है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja sees OM as the Lord's name — it is the first and highest name of the Lord. Chanting OM is worship of the Lord and the supreme means of meditating on Him.
vishisht.ins: OM is not a philosophical concept but a living name — the name by which the Lord calls Himself, and by which the devotee can call the Lord.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द ॐ को चेतना के सम्पूर्ण स्पेक्ट्रम का ध्वनि-प्रतिनिधित्व मानते हैं — अ (जाग्रत), उ (स्वप्न), म (सुषुप्ति), और मौन (तुरीय)। ॐ चेतना का मानचित्र है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads OM as the sonic representation of the entire spectrum of consciousness — A (waking), U (dream), M (deep sleep), and the silence (Turīya). OM is the map of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: OM is not merely a mantra to be chanted but a key to the architecture of consciousness — each sound opens a different chamber of awareness.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Yama answer Nachiketa's vast question with a single syllable?
dp.a: Nachiketa asked for the reality beyond all categories — beyond dharma, time, causation. The answer is not a philosophical treatise but a single sound: OM. This is deliberately paradoxical and profoundly meaningful. The Upanishadic teaching holds that ultimate reality cannot be captured by discursive thought — no amount of words, arguments, or descriptions can encompass the infinite. But a symbol can point beyond itself. OM is that symbol: it is the shortest possible utterance (a single syllable) that points to the vastest possible reality (Brahman). Saṅgraheṇa ('in brief') is the key word — Yama is not simplifying the truth but condensing it to its essence. The Māṇḍūkya Upanishad's entire twelve verses are an unpacking of this one syllable. The brevity of the answer honours the vastness of the truth: any longer answer would be more words about what words cannot reach.

dp.q: 🔍 How does this verse connect to the Bhagavad Gita?
dp.a: This verse is one of the most directly quoted Upanishadic passages in the Bhagavad Gita. In Gita 8.13, Krishna says: 'om ity ekākṣaraṁ brahma vyāharan mām anusmaran / yaḥ prayāti tyajan dehaṁ sa yāti paramāṁ gatim' — 'Uttering OM, the one-syllable Brahman, and remembering Me, whoever departs leaving the body, attains the supreme goal.' Krishna is directly echoing Yama's teaching to Nachiketa. The Gita also echoes the verse's structure: 'sarve vedā yat padam āmananti' finds its parallel in Gita 15.15: 'vedaiś ca sarvair aham eva vedyaḥ' — 'By all the Vedas, I alone am to be known.' The Katha verse established the principle; the Gita personalises it — the impersonal OM and the personal Lord (Krishna) converge as two faces of the same ultimate reality.

sk: एतद्ध्येवाक्षरं ब्रह्म एतद्ध्येवाक्षरं परम् | एतद्ध्येवाक्षरं ज्ञात्वा यो यदिच्छति तस्य तत् ||
ro: etad · hi · eva · akṣaraṁ · brahma · etad · hi · eva · akṣaraṁ · param | etad · hi · eva · akṣaraṁ · jñātvā · yo · yad · icchati · tasya · tat ||
hi: यह (ॐ) ही वह अक्षर (अविनाशी) ब्रह्म है; यही वह परम अक्षर है। इस अक्षर को जानकर जो जो चाहता है, उसे वही मिलता है।
en: This syllable (OM) is indeed Brahman. This syllable is indeed the Supreme. Having known this syllable, whatever one desires, that is theirs.

ws.e: the imperishable, the syllable — a+kṣara (that which does not perish); also means 'syllable,' creating a double meaning
Brahman — the ultimate reality
the supreme, the highest — nothing beyond this
having known — absolutive of √jñā; not heard or believed, but directly known
desires — √iṣ; whatever the knower wishes comes to them

gr: akṣaram — a brilliantly ambiguous word: it means both 'syllable' (referring to OM) and 'imperishable' (a+kṣara = that which does not decay). The verse exploits this double meaning: the syllable OM IS the imperishable Brahman. etad hi eva — 'this indeed is': the triple emphasis (etad + hi + eva) leaves no room for doubt. yo yad icchati tasya tat — 'whatever one desires, that is theirs': the paradox — the person who has transcended desire through knowledge receives everything.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.16 — The word akṣara carries a double meaning (syllable + imperishable) that is central to the Upanishadic theology of OM. The closing promise ('whatever one desires, that is theirs') echoes the Chāndogya Upanishad's 'satyakāma' (one whose desires are true).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'यो यदिच्छति तस्य तत्' — यह विरोधाभासी नहीं: जो ब्रह्म को जानता है, उसकी इच्छा ब्रह्म की इच्छा बन जाती है — इसलिए वह सदा पूर्ण होती है। वस्तुतः आत्मज्ञानी को कोई इच्छा शेष नहीं रहती।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'yo yad icchati tasya tat' is not contradictory: one who knows Brahman has their will aligned with Brahman's will — so it is always fulfilled. In reality, the knower of the Self has no remaining desires.
advaita.ins: When your will merges with the cosmic will, there is no gap between wanting and having — not because you get everything, but because you want only what is.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि ॐ में ब्रह्म = भगवान् विष्णु। 'यो यदिच्छति तस्य तत्' — भगवान् अपने भक्त की सब इच्छाएँ पूर्ण करते हैं, किन्तु सच्चा भक्त केवल भगवान् को ही चाहता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja identifies Brahman in OM with Lord Vishnu. 'Yo yad icchati tasya tat' — the Lord fulfils all desires of His devotee, but the true devotee desires only the Lord.
vishisht.ins: The ultimate gift is not getting what you want but wanting what the Lord gives — and what He gives is Himself.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि ॐ को 'जानना' बौद्धिक ज्ञान नहीं है — यह चेतना का उस स्तर तक उठना है जहाँ इच्छा और सत्ता एक हो जाते हैं। ऐसे ज्ञानी की इच्छा सृजन-शक्ति बन जाती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'knowing' OM is not intellectual knowledge — it is the elevation of consciousness to the level where will and being become one. The knower's desire becomes creative power.
aurobindo.ins: At the highest level, there is no difference between willing and being. The seer's thought is itself a creative act because it operates from the plane of truth.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the double meaning of 'akṣara'?
dp.a: The word akṣara carries two meanings that the verse deliberately merges: (1) syllable — a unit of sound, specifically referring to the syllable OM; (2) imperishable — a+kṣara, that which does not decay or perish, i.e., the eternal reality. By using this one word, the Upanishad asserts that the sound OM and the reality Brahman are not merely connected but identical. The syllable IS the imperishable. This is not metaphor — in the Vedic understanding, sound (śabda) is the primary medium of creation. The universe was created through sound (Vāk), and OM is the primordial sound from which all other sounds (and therefore all things) emerged. To know the syllable fully — not just to pronounce it but to understand it in its depth — is to know the imperishable reality from which everything comes.

dp.q: 🔍 How can the knower of Brahman 'get whatever they desire'?
dp.a: The promise 'yo yad icchati tasya tat' (whatever one desires, that is theirs) seems to contradict the entire teaching about transcending desire. The resolution lies in understanding what happens to desire in the knower. The Chāndogya Upanishad (8.1.5-6) explains: the knower of Brahman is called satyakāma (one whose desires are true) and satyasaṅkalpa (one whose intentions are real). This does not mean the sage desires worldly things and gets them — it means the sage's consciousness has risen to the level where desire and reality are identical. At the level of Brahman, there is no gap between willing and being — thought is creative, intention is manifestation. But practically, the sage who has realised Brahman desires nothing because they already are everything. The 'desire fulfilment' is a description of the ontological state, not a magical power: when you are the whole, what would you desire that you are not?

sk: एतदालम्बनं श्रेष्ठमेतदालम्बनं परम् | एतदालम्बनं ज्ञात्वा ब्रह्मलोके महीयते ||
ro: etad · ālambanam · śreṣṭham · etad · ālambanam · param | etad · ālambanam · jñātvā · brahmaloke · mahīyate ||
hi: यह (ॐ) सर्वश्रेष्ठ आलम्बन (सहारा) है; यही परम आलम्बन है। इस आलम्बन को जानकर (साधक) ब्रह्मलोक में महिमान्वित होता है।
en: This (OM) is the supreme support; this is the highest support. Knowing this support, one is glorified in the world of Brahman.

ws.e: support, prop, basis — ā+√lamb ('to hang from'); that which one holds onto for stability
the best, the finest — superlative; no better support exists
the highest — there is nothing beyond this
in the world of Brahman — the highest realm of existence

ws.h: महिमान्वित होता है, पूजित होता है
ws.e: is glorified, is honoured — passive of √mah ('to be great'); becomes great in the ultimate sense

gr: ālambanam — 'support': the metaphor is of a drowning person holding onto a rope, or a climber grasping a ledge. OM is that handhold for the soul traversing the ocean of saṁsāra. śreṣṭham ... param — 'best ... highest': superlatives heaped on superlatives. brahmaloke mahīyate — 'is glorified in Brahman's world': not merely enters but is honoured, celebrated.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.17 — OM as 'ālambana' (support) introduces the meditative function of the syllable — it is the anchor for the mind in contemplation. Brahmaloka here may mean either the world of the creator-god Brahmā or the state of Brahman-realisation.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'ब्रह्मलोक' यहाँ ब्रह्म-साक्षात्कार की अवस्था है, कोई भौगोलिक लोक नहीं। ॐ का ध्यान चित्त को ब्रह्म में स्थिर करता है — यही आलम्बन है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'brahmaloka' here is the state of Brahman-realisation, not a geographical world. OM-meditation stabilises the mind in Brahman — this is the support.
advaita.ins: The support is not external but internal — OM is the bridge between the restless mind and the still Brahman.

vishisht.h: रामानुज 'ब्रह्मलोक' को भगवान् के परमधाम (वैकुण्ठ) मानते हैं। ॐ के आश्रय से भक्त भगवान् के धाम में प्रतिष्ठित होता है — यह मुक्ति का चरम है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja reads 'brahmaloka' as the Lord's supreme abode (Vaikuṇṭha). Through the support of OM, the devotee is established in the Lord's eternal abode — this is the culmination of liberation.
vishisht.ins: OM is the devotee's passport to the eternal kingdom — the sound that carries the soul home.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'आलम्बन' को चेतना का स्थिरीकरण-बिन्दु मानते हैं — ध्यान में मन को ॐ पर टिकाने से चेतना उच्चतर स्तरों तक पहुँचती है। 'ब्रह्मलोक' = सत्-चित्-आनन्द की चेतना।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads 'ālambana' as the stabilisation-point of consciousness — by anchoring the mind on OM in meditation, consciousness ascends to higher planes. 'Brahmaloka' = the consciousness of Sat-Cit-Ānanda.
aurobindo.ins: OM is not a destination but a vehicle — the sound that lifts consciousness from the mental plane to the supramental.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is OM called a 'support' (ālambana)?
dp.a: The word ālambana (from ā+√lamb, 'to hang from, to lean upon') is a meditation term. In yogic practice, the mind needs an object to rest upon — without support, it scatters. OM serves as the supreme ālambana because it is simultaneously a sound (accessible to the senses) and Brahman itself (the ultimate reality). The meditator can begin by focusing on the audible sound 'OM' and gradually move through subtler and subtler levels until they arrive at the silence that lies beneath the sound — which is Brahman. OM is thus a bridge: it has one foot in the phenomenal world (as a sound) and one foot in the absolute (as Brahman). No other object of meditation has this dual nature, which is why it is called 'śreṣṭham' (the best) and 'param' (the highest) among all supports.

dp.q: 🔍 Does 'brahmaloka' mean a heavenly world or the state of liberation?
dp.a: The term brahmaloka is deliberately ambiguous and the three commentators read it differently. For Shankara, brahmaloka is not a place but a state of consciousness — the direct realisation of Brahman. There is nowhere to 'go' because Brahman is already everywhere; 'brahmaloka' simply means living in the awareness of Brahman. For Ramanuja, brahmaloka is a real, eternal realm — Vaikuṇṭha, the Lord's supreme abode — which the liberated soul enters after death, never to return. It is the permanent dwelling of the Lord and His devotees. For Aurobindo, brahmaloka is a plane of consciousness — the supramental plane of Sat-Cit-Ānanda — which can be accessed even while living in the body through the transformation of consciousness. Each reading is consistent with its tradition: non-dual (no separate world), devotional (an eternal divine realm), or integral (a consciousness-plane accessible through evolution).

sk: न जायते म्रियते वा विपश्चिन्नायं कुतश्चिन्न बभूव कश्चित् | अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ||
ro: na · jāyate · mriyate · vā · vipaścit · na · ayaṁ · kutaścit · na · babhūva · kaścit | ajaḥ · nityaḥ · śāśvato · ayaṁ · purāṇo · na · hanyate · hanyamāne · śarīre ||
hi: यह विपश्चित् (चेतन आत्मा) न जन्मता है, न मरता है। यह किसी से उत्पन्न नहीं हुआ, और इससे कोई उत्पन्न नहीं हुआ। यह अज (अजन्मा), नित्य, शाश्वत, पुरातन है — शरीर के नष्ट होने पर भी यह नष्ट नहीं होता।
en: The intelligent Self is not born, nor does it die. It did not come from anything, nor did anything come from it. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient — it is not slain when the body is slain.

ws.e: the intelligent one, the wise — vi+paścit; the Self that is consciousness itself
from anywhere — the Self has no origin, no source
became, came into being — perfect of √bhū; denied: it never 'became'
unborn — a+ja; never born, without origin
eternal — always existing, without beginning or end
everlasting — perpetually enduring

ws.s: न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे (na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre)
ws.h: शरीर मारे जाने पर भी नहीं मारा जाता
ws.e: is not slain when the body is slain — the Self survives the body's destruction

gr: na jāyate mriyate vā — 'neither born nor dies': two fundamental life-events negated. na ayaṁ kutaścit na babhūva kaścit — 'not from anything, nor anything from it': the Self is not an effect (it has no cause) and not a cause (nothing emerges from it in the causal sense). ajaḥ nityaḥ śāśvataḥ purāṇaḥ — four adjectives: unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient. na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre — the climactic statement: the body's death leaves the Self untouched.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.18 — This verse is quoted almost verbatim in the Bhagavad Gita (2.20). It is one of the most direct declarations of the Self's immortality in all of Indian scripture. The five negations systematically deny birth, death, origin, production, and destruction.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यह श्लोक आत्मा के पाँच विकारों (जन्म, अस्तित्व, वृद्धि, क्षय, मृत्यु) का निषेध करता है। जो अजन्मा है वह किसी के अधीन नहीं — वह स्वतन्त्र, अद्वितीय, निर्विकार ब्रह्म है।
advaita.en: Shankara says this verse negates the five modifications (vikāra) of the Self: birth, existence, growth, decay, death. What is unborn is subject to nothing — it is the independent, unique, changeless Brahman.
advaita.ins: If the Self were born, it could die. If it could die, liberation would be temporary. The Upanishad insists: you were never born — therefore you can never die.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि जीवात्मा शाश्वत है — यह भगवान् का अंश है और भगवान् के समान अविनाशी है। 'न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे' — शरीर नश्वर है पर आत्मा शाश्वत — इसलिए शरीर की मृत्यु आत्मा की मृत्यु नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the jīvātman is eternal — it is a part of the Lord and imperishable like the Lord. 'Na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre' — the body is perishable but the soul is eternal — therefore the body's death is not the soul's death.
vishisht.ins: Death is a costume change, not an extinction. The soul sheds the body as one sheds worn-out clothes — the wearer remains.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि 'विपश्चित्' शब्द महत्त्वपूर्ण है — आत्मा मात्र 'सत्ता' नहीं, यह 'चेतन सत्ता' है — ज्ञान इसका स्वभाव है। शरीर की मृत्यु चेतना की एक अभिव्यक्ति का अन्त है, चेतना का नहीं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo notes that 'vipaścit' is significant — the Self is not mere 'existence' but 'conscious existence' — knowledge is its nature. The body's death is the end of one expression of consciousness, not of consciousness itself.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness does not depend on the body; the body depends on consciousness. When the instrument breaks, the player remains.

dp.q: 🔍 How does this verse appear in the Bhagavad Gita?
dp.a: This verse is reproduced almost word-for-word in Bhagavad Gita 2.20: 'na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ / ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre.' The Gita adds 'kadācin' (at any time) and 'bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ' (having been, it will not cease to be), making the temporal denial even more explicit. Krishna is speaking to Arjuna who grieves over killing his kinsmen in battle — and the message is identical to Yama's: the Self cannot be killed, so grief over physical death is based on a misunderstanding. The direct borrowing shows that the Gita sees itself as continuous with the Upanishadic tradition, not as a separate teaching. The Katha is the source; the Gita is its most famous application.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the philosophical significance of 'na ayaṁ kutaścit' (not from anything)?
dp.a: The phrase 'na ayaṁ kutaścit' ('this did not come from anywhere') makes a radical ontological claim: the Self has no origin. It is not a product, not an effect, not an emanation, not a creation. It did not evolve from matter, it was not breathed into the body by a creator-god, it did not emerge from anything else. This distinguishes the Upanishadic view from both creationism (God created souls) and materialism (consciousness emerged from matter). The Self simply IS — beginningless, uncaused, self-existent. The companion phrase 'na babhūva kaścit' ('nothing came from it') adds that the Self is also not a cause of anything else — it does not produce, create, or generate. This seems contradictory to the Upanishadic teaching that 'from this Self, space arose' (Taittirīya 2.1) — but Shankara resolves this by saying the Self appears to create through māyā while remaining unchanged itself, like a rope that appears to be a snake.

sk: हन्ता चेन्मन्यते हन्तुं हतश्चेन्मन्यते हतम् | उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते ||
ro: hantā · cet · manyate · hantuṁ · hataś · cet · manyate · hatam | ubhau · tau · na · vijānīto · na · ayaṁ · hanti · na · hanyate ||
hi: यदि कोई मारने वाला (हन्ता) सोचता है कि 'मैं मारता हूँ' और मारा जाने वाला (हत) सोचता है कि 'मैं मारा गया' — तो वे दोनों नहीं जानते। यह (आत्मा) न मारता है, न मारा जाता है।
en: If the slayer thinks 'I slay' and the slain thinks 'I am slain,' both do not know. This (Self) neither slays nor is slain.

ws.e: the slayer — agent noun from √han ('to kill')
to slay — infinitive of √han
the slain — past participle of √han
understand — vi+√jñā; dual number: neither of the two knows
does not slay — the Self is not an agent of action
is not slain — the Self is not an object of action

gr: hantā cet manyate hantum — 'if the killer thinks he kills': the verb manyate (thinks, believes) is crucial — it implies the belief is false. ubhau tau na vijānītaḥ — 'both of them do not know': dual number verb; both parties are equally ignorant. na ayaṁ hanti na hanyate — 'this neither kills nor is killed': the Self is beyond agency and patiency — it neither does nor has done to it.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.19 — This verse appears verbatim in the Bhagavad Gita (2.19) and is originally from the Rig Veda. It establishes that the Self transcends the categories of agent (kartā) and object (karma) — it is the actionless witness.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि आत्मा न कर्ता (doer) है न भोक्ता (experiencer)। 'मैं मारता हूँ' या 'मैं मारा गया' — ये दोनों अहंकार के भ्रम हैं। आत्मा अक्रिय (actionless) साक्षी है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the Self is neither the doer (kartā) nor the experiencer (bhoktā). 'I kill' or 'I am killed' — both are delusions of the ego (ahaṁkāra). The Self is the actionless witness.
advaita.ins: All sense of agency — 'I do this, I suffer that' — belongs to the ego, not to the Self. The Self is the unchanging witness of all action.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि जीवात्मा स्वभाव से अक्रिय है — कर्तृत्व प्रकृति (शरीर-मन) का है। 'हन्ता' और 'हत' दोनों शरीर के विषय में कहे जाते हैं, आत्मा के नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the jīvātman is by nature actionless — agency belongs to prakṛti (body-mind). 'Slayer' and 'slain' apply to the body, not to the soul.
vishisht.ins: The soul acts through the body as a driver acts through a vehicle — the vehicle can be damaged, but the driver within remains.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि 'मन्यते' (सोचता है) शब्द महत्त्वपूर्ण है — मारना-मरना मन के स्तर पर है; आत्मा के स्तर पर न कोई कर्ता है, न कर्म। चेतना का यह साक्षी-भाव ही मुक्ति है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo notes 'manyate' (thinks) is crucial — killing and being killed occur at the mental level; at the level of the Self, there is no doer, no deed. This witness-consciousness is liberation itself.
aurobindo.ins: The identification with action — 'I am the doer' — is the knot that ties consciousness to the body. Untie it, and you are free.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the practical implication of 'the Self neither kills nor is killed'?
dp.a: This teaching does NOT mean that killing is morally neutral — it means that the true Self (Atman) is not the agent of any action. All action belongs to the body-mind complex (the vehicle of prakṛti), not to the Self that witnesses through it. The practical implications: (1) Ethically — karma still operates at the level of the body-mind; one still bears consequences for action. The teaching liberates one from existential horror, not from moral responsibility. (2) Psychologically — the fear of death is based on the false identification of Self with body. When one knows 'I am not the body,' the fear of death dissolves. (3) In the Gita's context — Krishna uses this verse to tell Arjuna that his grief is misplaced: the warriors he will 'kill' cannot be killed in their essence. The bodies fall; the Selves are untouched. This is not a licence to kill but a correction of Arjuna's metaphysical confusion.

dp.q: 🔍 How does this verse connect to the concept of the witness (sākṣī)?
dp.a: The verse establishes the Self as the sākṣī (witness) — pure consciousness that observes without participating. The key insight: agency ('I kill') and patiency ('I am killed') are both forms of identification with action. The Self is beyond both. It is not the hand that strikes, not the body that falls, not the mind that decides, not the emotion that grieves. It is the awareness in which all of this appears. The Sāṅkhya philosophy formalises this: puruṣa (consciousness) is eternally distinct from prakṛti (nature/matter), which alone acts. The Gita (3.27-28) states: 'All actions are performed by the guṇas of prakṛti; the Self, deluded by ahaṁkāra, thinks: I am the doer.' When the Self recognises its own witness-nature, the false sense of agency drops — and with it, the entire edifice of karma, fear, and suffering built on that false sense.

sk: अणोरणीयान्महतो महीयानात्माऽस्य जन्तोर्निहितो गुहायाम् | तमक्रतुः पश्यति वीतशोको धातुप्रसादान्महिमानमात्मनः ||
ro: aṇoḥ · aṇīyān · mahato · mahīyān · ātmā · asya · jantoḥ · nihito · guhāyām | tam · akratuḥ · paśyati · vītaśoko · dhātuprasādāt · mahimānam · ātmanaḥ ||
hi: अणु से भी सूक्ष्म, महान् से भी महान् — यह आत्मा इस जीव के हृदय-गुहा में छिपा है। जो निष्काम (अक्रतु) और शोकरहित (वीतशोक) है, वह अन्तःकरण की प्रसन्नता (धातुप्रसाद) से आत्मा की महिमा को देखता है।
en: Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great — the Self is hidden in the heart-cave of this living being. One who is free from desire and free from sorrow sees the majesty of the Self through the serenity of the inner faculties.

ws.e: subtler than the subtle — comparative: smaller than the smallest conceivable thing
greater than the great — comparative: larger than the largest
placed, hidden — ni+√dhā ('to place'); the Self is deposited in the heart-cave
in the cave — the heart as the secret chamber of the Self
without desire, without volition — a+kratu; one whose desires have been stilled
free from sorrow — vīta (gone) + śoka (grief); grief has departed
through the serenity of the inner faculties — dhātu (constituent elements, faculties) + prasāda (clarity, grace, serenity)

gr: aṇoḥ aṇīyān mahato mahīyān — the most famous paradox of the Upanishads: the Self is simultaneously the smallest and the largest. It is not a 'size' but pervades all scales. dhātuprasādāt — 'by the grace/serenity of the dhātus': Shankara reads dhātu as the mind and senses; when they are clear and tranquil, the Self becomes visible. akratuḥ vītaśokaḥ — two preconditions: absence of desire and absence of grief.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.20 — This is one of the most celebrated verses in all Upanishadic literature. The paradox 'subtler than the subtle, greater than the great' appears in multiple Upanishads (Śvetāśvatara 3.20, Muṇḍaka 3.1.7). 'Dhātuprasāda' is a key concept — the Self is seen not through effort but through the natural clarity of a purified mind.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'अणोः अणीयान्' — आत्मा इसलिए सूक्ष्मतम है क्योंकि वह निराकार, निर्गुण है; 'महतो महीयान्' — सर्वव्यापी होने से सबसे बड़ा है। 'धातुप्रसाद' = अन्तःकरण की शुद्धि — जब मन स्वच्छ दर्पण बनता है, तभी आत्मा का प्रतिबिम्ब दिखता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'aṇoḥ aṇīyān' — the Self is the subtlest because it is formless and attributeless; 'mahato mahīyān' — the greatest because it is all-pervading. 'Dhātuprasāda' = purity of the inner organ — when the mind becomes a clear mirror, the Self's reflection appears.
advaita.ins: The Self is already here — the only obstacle is the turbidity of the mind. Purify the mind, and the Self shines by its own light.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् अणु में भी अणु रूप से (अन्तर्यामी) और ब्रह्माण्ड में भी विराट रूप से विद्यमान हैं। 'धातुप्रसाद' = भगवान् की कृपा — जब भगवान् प्रसन्न होते हैं तभी आत्म-दर्शन होता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord is present as the subtle inner controller (antaryāmī) even within the atom, and as the cosmic form (Virāṭ) in the entire universe. 'Dhātuprasāda' = the Lord's grace — only when the Lord is pleased does Self-vision occur.
vishisht.ins: The Lord is simultaneously within the smallest atom and beyond the largest cosmos — His presence has no limits, and realising Him requires His grace, not merely human effort.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'अणोः अणीयान् महतो महीयान्' में चेतना की अनन्त पैमाने देखते हैं — आत्मा एक साथ सूक्ष्मतम और विराटतम है क्योंकि चेतना आकार से बँधी नहीं। 'धातुप्रसाद' — चेतना की आन्तरिक शान्ति ही दर्शन का द्वार है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees in 'aṇoḥ aṇīyān mahato mahīyān' the infinite scalability of consciousness — the Self is simultaneously the subtlest and the vastest because consciousness is not bound by size. 'Dhātuprasāda' — the inner peace of consciousness is the doorway to vision.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness is not a thing with a size — it is the dimensionless ground of all dimensions. It can focus to a point finer than an atom or expand to contain universes.

dp.q: 🔍 How can the Self be both 'subtler than the subtle' and 'greater than the great'?
dp.a: The paradox aṇoḥ aṇīyān mahato mahīyān is not a contradiction but a statement about the nature of consciousness. Physical objects have a determinate size — an atom is small, a galaxy is large, and neither can be both. But the Self is not a physical object; it is consciousness, and consciousness has no inherent size. It can focus to a point so fine that it is within the smallest particle (this is the Self as antaryāmī, the inner controller), and it can expand to encompass everything that exists (this is the Self as Brahman, the cosmic totality). The paradox expresses the fact that the Self transcends the category of size altogether. It is not 'very small' or 'very large' but beyond the dimension of magnitude. Any attempt to locate it at a particular scale fails because it is present at every scale simultaneously. This is experientially verifiable in deep meditation: consciousness can contract to a pinpoint or expand without limit.

dp.q: 🔍 What is 'dhātuprasāda' and how does it enable seeing the Self?
dp.a: Dhātuprasāda is a compound of dhātu (the constituent elements — here meaning the mind, intellect, and senses) and prasāda (clarity, serenity, grace). The word prasāda carries a double meaning: (1) clarity — like clear water through which one can see the bottom; (2) grace — a gift, something bestowed rather than earned. The teaching is: the Self is not seen through effort, strain, or intellectual gymnastics. It is seen when the inner instruments become naturally serene — clear, still, settled. This is why the verse pairs two preconditions: akratuḥ (freedom from desire) and vītaśokaḥ (freedom from sorrow). Desire agitates the mind; sorrow clouds it. When both are absent, the mind settles into its natural clarity — and in that clarity, the Self is simply seen, the way one sees the moon in a still pond. The seeing requires no special technique — only the removal of what obstructs it.

sk: आसीनो दूरं व्रजति शयानो याति सर्वतः | कस्तं मदामदं देवं मदन्यो ज्ञातुमर्हति ||
ro: āsīno · dūraṁ · vrajati · śayāno · yāti · sarvataḥ | kas · taṁ · madāmadam · devaṁ · mad · anyo · jñātum · arhati ||
hi: बैठा हुआ दूर तक जाता है; लेटा हुआ सब ओर पहुँचता है। उस आनन्दमय और आनन्दरहित (मदामद) देव (आत्मा) को मुझ (यम) से भिन्न कौन जान सकता है?
en: Sitting, it travels far; lying down, it goes everywhere. Who other than me (Yama) is fit to know that God who is both joy and the absence of joy?

ws.e: sitting, stationary — present participle of √ās; the Self is motionless
travels far — though stationary, it reaches everywhere
lying down — present participle of √śī; at perfect rest
goes everywhere — pervades all directions while perfectly still

ws.h: आनन्दमय और आनन्दरहित, हर्ष और विषाद से परे
ws.e: joy and non-joy — mada (intoxication, joy) + amada (non-joy); beyond the duality of elation and depression
the shining one, the divine — the Self as luminous consciousness

gr: āsīno dūraṁ vrajati śayāno yāti sarvataḥ — two paradoxes: 'sitting, travels far' and 'lying, goes everywhere.' The Self is motionless yet omnipresent — it does not move because it is already everywhere. madāmadam — 'joy-and-non-joy': a bahuvrihi compound; the Self both IS joy and transcends joy. mad anyaḥ — 'other than me': Yama, as the Lord of Death, claims unique qualification to know the Self.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.21 — The paradox of motion-in-stillness echoes the Isha Upanishad (4-5). 'Madāmadam' is a subtle compound — the Self is the source of joy but is itself beyond the joy-sorrow duality. Yama's claim 'who other than me can know this' is either exclusive (only Death knows the deathless) or rhetorical.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'आसीनो दूरं व्रजति' — आत्मा गतिरहित है किन्तु सर्वव्यापी है, इसलिए 'दूर तक जाना' कहा गया। जैसे आकाश सब ओर है पर हिलता नहीं — वैसे ही आत्मा।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'āsīno dūraṁ vrajati' — the Self is motionless yet all-pervading, so it is said to 'travel far.' Just as space is everywhere but does not move — so too the Self.
advaita.ins: Movement implies going from here to there. The Self is already 'there' — it does not move because there is no place where it is not.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् अपने परमधाम में विराजमान होते हुए भी अन्तर्यामी रूप से सर्वत्र व्याप्त हैं। 'मदामदम्' — भगवान् आनन्द-स्वरूप हैं पर सांसारिक सुख-दुःख से परे हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord, while seated in His supreme abode, pervades everywhere as the inner controller. 'Madāmadam' — the Lord is bliss itself but beyond worldly pleasure and pain.
vishisht.ins: The Lord does not need to travel to be present — His presence is not limited by location. He is both 'here' in the heart and 'there' in His eternal abode.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'आसीनो दूरं व्रजति' में चेतना की प्रकृति देखते हैं — शरीर स्थिर है पर चेतना दूर तक पहुँचती है (जैसे ध्यान में)। आत्मा स्थान से बँधी नहीं — वह स्थान का मूल है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees in 'āsīno dūraṁ vrajati' the nature of consciousness — the body is stationary but consciousness reaches far (as in meditation). The Self is not bound by space — it is the source of space.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness is non-local by nature — it does not need to physically travel to be present at a distance. In deep meditation, this becomes direct experience.

dp.q: 🔍 How can something be motionless yet travel everywhere?
dp.a: The paradox 'sitting, it travels far; lying, it goes everywhere' describes the nature of consciousness versus matter. A physical body must move through space to be in a different place — but consciousness is not physical. The Self does not 'travel' by leaving one place and arriving at another; it is simultaneously present everywhere. The Isha Upanishad (4-5) states the same truth: 'It moves; It does not move. It is far; It is near.' The resolution: at the level of the body, there is movement and location. At the level of the Self, there is neither — because the Self is the space in which movement occurs. A container does not move when its contents move. The Self is the ultimate container — the space of consciousness in which all objects, including the body, appear and move. It 'sits' because it is still; it 'travels far' because nothing is outside it.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'madāmadam' (joy-and-non-joy) mean?
dp.a: Madāmadam is a bahuvrihi compound: mada (joy, intoxication, rapture) + amada (non-joy, sobriety). The Self is described as both: it IS joy (the Taittirīya Upanishad declares 'ānando brahmeti — Brahman is bliss') and it TRANSCENDS joy (it is not subject to the fluctuation between elation and depression). How can something be joy and non-joy simultaneously? Because the Self is not the experiential emotion of happiness (which comes and goes) but the ground of all experience. It is the bliss that underlies both happiness and unhappiness — the peace that remains unchanged whether the surface is joyful or sorrowful. The closest analogy is the ocean: the surface may be stormy or calm, but the deep water is always still. The Self is that deep stillness — it is not 'happy' in the way a person is happy after good news, but it is the foundational peace from which all experience arises.

sk: अशरीरं शरीरेष्वनवस्थेष्ववस्थितम् | महान्तं विभुमात्मानं मत्वा धीरो न शोचति ||
ro: aśarīraṁ · śarīreṣu · anavastheṣu · avasthitam | mahāntaṁ · vibhum · ātmānaṁ · matvā · dhīro · na · śocati ||
hi: शरीरों में (रहते हुए भी) शरीररहित, अस्थिर (नाशवान्) शरीरों में स्थित (अचल), उस महान्, सर्वव्यापी आत्मा को जानकर धीर (विवेकी) पुरुष शोक नहीं करता।
en: Bodiless among bodies, stable among the unstable — having known the Self as great and all-pervading, the wise one does not grieve.

ws.e: bodiless — a+śarīra; without a body; the Self has no physical form
among bodies — locative plural; the Self resides in all bodies yet has no body of its own
in the unstable, impermanent — an+avastha; the bodies are constantly changing
firmly established — ava+√sthā; perfectly steady amid the flux
great — not in size but in significance and scope
all-pervading — vi+√bhū; present everywhere simultaneously
does not grieve — √śuc; sorrow is eliminated by knowledge

gr: aśarīraṁ śarīreṣu — 'bodiless among bodies': the paradox is compressed into two words — the Self lives in bodies but IS NOT a body. anavastheṣu avasthitam — 'stable among the unstable': another paradox — the bodies change, decay, and die; the Self within them is unchanging. na śocati — 'does not grieve': the practical fruit of Self-knowledge — freedom from sorrow.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.22 — The paradoxes (bodiless/in-bodies, stable/among-the-unstable) concisely express the relationship between the unchanging Self and the changing body. The conclusion 'does not grieve' connects metaphysical knowledge to psychological liberation. This echoes the Gita's 'na śocati na kāṅkṣati' (18.54).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'अशरीरं शरीरेषु' — आत्मा शरीर में है पर शरीर का नहीं, जैसे आकाश घड़े में है पर घड़े का नहीं। शोक अज्ञान का फल है; ज्ञान से शोक का नाश होता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'aśarīraṁ śarīreṣu' — the Self is in the body but not of the body, as space is in the pot but not of the pot. Grief is the fruit of ignorance; knowledge destroys grief.
advaita.ins: Grief comes from identifying with what changes. Know yourself as the unchanging, and grief has no ground to stand on.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् सब शरीरों में अन्तर्यामी के रूप में हैं पर शरीर की सीमाओं से अछूते हैं। जो इसे जानता है वह शोक करने का कारण नहीं पाता — क्योंकि जो वस्तुतः मरता ही नहीं, उसके लिए शोक क्यों?
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord is in all bodies as the inner controller but untouched by bodily limitations. One who knows this finds no cause for grief — for why grieve for that which never truly dies?
vishisht.ins: When you know that the soul is untouched by what happens to the body, grief loses its foundation — not by suppression but by understanding.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'अनवस्थेषु अवस्थितम्' में विकास (evolution) का सिद्धान्त देखते हैं — शरीर बदलते हैं (विकसित होते हैं), पर उनके भीतर की चेतना स्थिर और शाश्वत है। 'न शोचति' — मृत्यु का भय विकास का ब्रेक है; ज्ञान उसे हटा देता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads 'anavastheṣu avasthitam' as reflecting evolution — bodies change (evolve), but the consciousness within them is stable and eternal. 'Na śocati' — the fear of death is evolution's brake; knowledge releases it.
aurobindo.ins: The body is a temporary instrument of consciousness — when the instrument is worn out, consciousness takes a new one. There is nothing to grieve in changing instruments.

dp.q: 🔍 How does knowing the Self eliminate grief?
dp.a: The verse's conclusion — na śocati (does not grieve) — is not a moral injunction ('you should not grieve') but a natural consequence of knowledge ('you WILL NOT grieve'). Grief arises from perceived loss: 'I have lost someone/something precious.' But if the Self is unborn, undying, bodiless, all-pervading, and eternal (as the preceding verses establish), then what has been 'lost'? The body changes — but you are not the body. The mind suffers — but you are not the mind. Someone dies — but the Self does not die. Grief is the product of a misidentification: taking the temporary for the permanent, the body for the Self. When this misidentification is corrected through knowledge, grief dissolves — not because one becomes callous or indifferent, but because the metaphysical basis of grief (the belief that something real has been destroyed) is seen to be false. The wise person may still feel the natural sorrow of parting, but the existential horror of death — 'they are gone forever, and I too will be gone' — evaporates.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'bodiless among bodies' (aśarīraṁ śarīreṣu) mean?
dp.a: The phrase aśarīraṁ śarīreṣu is a compressed statement of the Self's relationship to embodiment. The Self inhabits bodies but does not possess one — it is bodiless (aśarīra) by nature, even while being present in bodies (śarīreṣu). Shankara's analogy: space is in a pot but is not the pot's space. When the pot breaks, the space inside does not break — it was never the pot's property; it was simply present where the pot happened to be. Similarly, when a body dies, the Self within it is untouched — it was never the body's Self; it was simply present in the body. The further paradox anavastheṣu avasthitam (stable among the unstable) deepens this: the bodies are constantly changing — growing, aging, decaying — while the Self within them is perfectly still and constant. It is the one unchanging reality in a universe of change.

sk: नायमात्मा प्रवचनेन लभ्यो न मेधया न बहुना श्रुतेन | यमेवैष वृणुते तेन लभ्यस्तस्यैष आत्मा विवृणुते तनूं स्वाम् ||
ro: na · ayam · ātmā · pravacanena · labhyo · na · medhayā · na · bahunā · śrutena | yam · eva · eṣa · vṛṇute · tena · labhyas · tasya · eṣa · ātmā · vivṛṇute · tanūṁ · svām ||
hi: यह आत्मा न प्रवचन से प्राप्त होता है, न मेधा (बुद्धि) से, न बहुत श्रवण से। जिसे यह (आत्मा) स्वयं चुनता है, उसी को यह प्राप्त होता है — उसके लिए यह आत्मा अपना स्वरूप प्रकट करता है।
en: This Self cannot be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much learning. It is gained only by the one whom it chooses — to such a one the Self reveals its own form.

ws.e: by instruction, by discourse — even the best teaching cannot by itself produce realisation
by intelligence, by intellectual power — even the sharpest mind cannot grasp the Self as an object
by much hearing/learning — bahunā śrutena: even extensive study of scriptures is insufficient
chooses, selects — √vṛ (middle voice); the Self chooses the seeker
reveals, uncovers — vi+√vṛ; the Self unveils its own form
its own form — tanū (body, form) + svā (own); the Self shows itself as it really is

gr: na pravacanena, na medhayā, na bahunā śrutena — three negations: not by teaching, not by intellect, not by learning. These deny all conventional means of knowledge. yam eva eṣa vṛṇute — 'whom this (Self) chooses': the passive seeker is chosen by the active Self. The verb vṛṇute is middle voice, suggesting the Self acts for its own purpose. vivṛṇute tanūṁ svām — 'reveals its own form': the Self does not merely become known but actively unveils itself to the chosen one.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.23 — One of the most quoted and debated verses in Vedantic philosophy. The claim that the Self 'chooses' whom it reveals itself to raises the question of grace vs. effort. This verse appears also in the Mundaka Upanishad (3.2.3) almost identically.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'वृणुते' (चुनता है) का अर्थ है — जो साधक तीव्र मुमुक्षा (मोक्ष की प्रबल इच्छा) से आत्मा को चाहता है, आत्मा उसे चुनती है। यह पारस्परिक है — साधक आत्मा को चुनता है, आत्मा साधक को चुनती है।
advaita.en: Shankara reads 'vṛṇute' (chooses) as: the Self chooses the seeker who yearns for it with intense mumukṣā (desire for liberation). It is reciprocal — the seeker chooses the Self, and the Self chooses the seeker.
advaita.ins: Self-realisation is not a one-sided effort — it is a meeting. The seeker reaches toward the Self, and the Self reaches toward the seeker. Neither alone is sufficient.

vishisht.h: रामानुज के लिए यह श्लोक ईश्वर-कृपा (divine grace) का सर्वोच्च प्रमाण है। भगवान् 'वृणुते' — वे स्वयं चुनते हैं किसे मुक्ति मिलेगी। शरणागति (surrender) ही वह माध्यम है जिससे भगवान् का चुनाव प्राप्त किया जाता है।
vishisht.en: For Ramanuja, this verse is the supreme proof of divine grace (īśvara-kṛpā). The Lord 'vṛṇute' — He Himself chooses whom He will liberate. Śaraṇāgati (surrender) is the means by which the Lord's choice is obtained.
vishisht.ins: Liberation is ultimately a gift, not an achievement. The devotee's role is to surrender completely — the Lord's role is to choose and reveal.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि 'वृणुते' — आत्मा का 'चुनना' — का अर्थ है कि चेतना का उच्चतर स्तर (Higher Self) निम्नतर स्तर (surface self) को तब स्वीकार करता है जब वह तैयार होता है। यह कृपा नहीं, चेतना की प्राकृतिक प्रक्रिया है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'vṛṇute' — the Self's 'choosing' — means the higher consciousness (Higher Self) accepts the lower self (surface self) when it is ready. This is not arbitrary grace but the natural process of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The Self does not randomly choose favourites — it reveals itself to consciousness that has prepared itself to receive the revelation. Readiness IS the grace.

dp.q: 🔍 Does the Self really 'choose' some people and reject others?
dp.a: The phrase 'yam eva eṣa vṛṇute tena labhyaḥ' ('it is gained only by the one whom it chooses') has generated centuries of debate. Does it mean the Self is arbitrary, favouring some and ignoring others? The three traditions offer different readings. Shankara resolves the apparent arbitrariness: the Self 'chooses' the one who has made themselves ready through viveka, vairāgya, and intense mumukṣā. The choosing is mutual — the seeker's intense longing is the Self's response. Ramanuja takes the choosing literally: it is the Lord's grace, freely given — but the Lord is not arbitrary; He responds to the devotee's surrender (prapatti). Aurobindo reads it as a natural process: the higher consciousness descends when the lower consciousness is ready to receive it, like water flowing to the lowest point. All three agree on one thing: it cannot be forced by intellectual effort alone. The three negations (no instruction, no intellect, no learning) make this clear — the standard means of knowledge are necessary but not sufficient. Something more is needed: call it grace, readiness, or the ripeness of the soul.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'vivṛṇute tanūṁ svām' (reveals its own form) mean?
dp.a: The phrase vivṛṇute tanūṁ svām is extraordinary: the Self reveals its own body/form (tanū = body, form; svām = its own). This means Self-knowledge is not constructed by the mind but shown by the Self itself. The verb vivṛṇute (from vi+√vṛ, 'to uncover') means 'unveils' — like removing a cloth from a sculpture. The sculpture was always there; the unveiling does not create it but makes it visible. This has profound implications for the epistemology of Self-knowledge: (1) The Self is not an object of knowledge that the mind grasps — it is a subject that reveals itself. (2) The revelation is of the Self's own form (svām tanūm) — not a description, concept, or image, but the Self as it actually is. (3) The process is active on the Self's side — the Self is not passive data waiting to be processed; it is a living reality that shows itself when conditions are right. This is why all the great Upanishadic teachers say that Self-knowledge is fundamentally different from all other knowledge — it is not acquisition but revelation.

sk: नाविरतो दुश्चरितान्नाशान्तो नासमाहितः | नाशान्तमानसो वाऽपि प्रज्ञानेनैनमाप्नुयात् ||
ro: na · avirataḥ · duścaritāt · na · aśānto · na · asamāhitaḥ | na · aśāntamānaso · vā · api · prajñānena · enam · āpnuyāt ||
hi: जो दुराचार से विरत नहीं हुआ, जो शान्त नहीं है, जो समाहित (एकाग्र) नहीं है, जिसका मन शान्त नहीं है — वह प्रज्ञान (ज्ञान) से भी इस (आत्मा) को नहीं पा सकता।
en: One who has not turned away from bad conduct, who is not tranquil, who is not concentrated, whose mind is not at peace — such a one cannot attain this (Self) even through knowledge.

ws.h: विरत न हुआ, न रुका हुआ
ws.e: not ceased, not turned away — a+virata; one who has not stopped wrongdoing
from bad conduct — duś+carita; unethical behaviour
not tranquil — the senses are not subdued
not concentrated — a+samāhita; the mind is scattered
whose mind is not at peace — aśānta (unpeaceful) + mānasa (mind)
by knowledge, by wisdom — even knowledge is insufficient without the proper inner state

gr: na avirataḥ duścaritāt — four negations specify what disqualifies: (1) not turned from bad conduct, (2) not tranquil, (3) not concentrated, (4) mind not at peace. Each targets a different level: ethics, senses, intellect, mind. prajñānena enam āpnuyāt — 'could attain this through knowledge': even knowledge (prajñāna) is powerless when the four prerequisites are absent.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.24 — This verse establishes the ethical and psychological prerequisites for Self-knowledge. It balances verse 23 (the Self chooses) with concrete requirements: right conduct, sensory calm, mental concentration, inner peace. Knowledge without these prerequisites is barren.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यह श्लोक साधन-चतुष्टय (चार योग्यताएँ) को संक्षेप में बताता है: शम (इन्द्रिय-निग्रह), दम (मन-निग्रह), उपरति (विषय-त्याग), समाधान (चित्त-एकाग्रता)। बिना इनके शास्त्र-ज्ञान भी मुक्ति नहीं दे सकता।
advaita.en: Shankara says this verse summarises the sādhana-catuṣṭaya (four qualifications): śama (sense-control), dama (mind-control), uparati (withdrawal), samādhāna (concentration). Without these, even scriptural knowledge cannot liberate.
advaita.ins: Knowledge is the lamp, but the prerequisites are the steady hand that holds it. Without ethical discipline and mental calm, even the brightest lamp flickers and fails to illuminate.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् उसी को चुनते हैं जो आचरण में शुद्ध है, मन में शान्त है, और हृदय में एकाग्र है। ये गुण शरणागति के अंग हैं — भगवान् की कृपा इन्हीं को मिलती है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord chooses one who is pure in conduct, peaceful in mind, and concentrated in heart. These qualities are aspects of surrender — the Lord's grace comes to those who possess them.
vishisht.ins: Grace is not random — it flows to prepared hearts. The preparation is ethical living, inner tranquillity, and focused devotion.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द इसमें साधना के व्यावहारिक पक्ष को देखते हैं — आध्यात्मिक ज्ञान बौद्धिक जानकारी नहीं, चेतना का रूपान्तरण है। रूपान्तरण के लिए अन्तःकरण की शुद्धि, शान्ति, और एकाग्रता अनिवार्य है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees the practical side of sādhana — spiritual knowledge is not intellectual information but transformation of consciousness. For transformation, purification, peace, and concentration of the inner being are indispensable.
aurobindo.ins: You cannot pour clarity into a turbulent vessel. The mind must be stilled, the conduct purified, the attention gathered — only then can the truth of the Self be received.

dp.q: 🔍 What are the four prerequisites for Self-knowledge according to this verse?
dp.a: The verse specifies four disqualifications, which imply four prerequisites: (1) Virati from duścarita — cessation of bad conduct. The seeker must live ethically; otherwise the mind is too disturbed by guilt, fear, and their consequences to settle into contemplation. (2) Śānti — tranquillity of the senses. The senses must be withdrawn from their habitual pursuit of objects — not suppressed violently but naturally quieted. (3) Samādhāna — concentration, one-pointedness. The intellect must be able to hold a single thought or inquiry steadily without scattering. (4) Śāntamānasa — peace of mind. The deepest layer: the mind itself must be at peace, free from anxiety, desire, and agitation. These four form a progression from the coarsest (external behaviour) to the subtlest (internal peace). They correspond roughly to the sādhana-catuṣṭaya of classical Vedanta and to the first four limbs of Patañjali's yoga (yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma — ethics, discipline, stability, breath-control).

dp.q: 🔍 Why can knowledge (prajñāna) alone not lead to realisation?
dp.a: The verse makes a startling claim: even knowledge (prajñāna) is insufficient without ethical and psychological preparation. This seems to contradict the Advaitic principle that 'knowledge alone liberates' (jñānād eva kaivalyam). The resolution: prajñāna here means theoretical, intellectual knowledge — understanding the teaching conceptually. The Upanishad is saying that understanding is not the same as realising. A person may read every Upanishad, master every argument, and still not attain Self-knowledge — because Self-knowledge is not a thought but a state of being. The prerequisites (ethics, calm, concentration, inner peace) do not produce knowledge; they remove the obstacles to it. The Self is already present and self-luminous (svayam-prakāśa) — what hides it is the turbulence of the unethical, agitated, scattered mind. Clear the turbulence, and the Self shines of its own accord. The prerequisites are not additional requirements but the removal of obstructions — like clearing clouds from the sun.

sk: यस्य ब्रह्म च क्षत्रं च उभे भवत ओदनः | मृत्युर्यस्योपसेचनं क इत्था वेद यत्र सः ||
ro: yasya · brahma · ca · kṣatraṁ · ca · ubhe · bhavataḥ · odanaḥ | mṛtyuḥ · yasya · upasecanaṁ · ka · itthā · veda · yatra · saḥ ||
hi: जिसके लिए ब्राह्मण और क्षत्रिय दोनों भात (भोजन) के समान हैं, और मृत्यु जिसकी चटनी (उपसेचन) है — भला कौन जानता है कि वह (आत्मा) कहाँ है?
en: For whom the Brahmin and the warrior are both like food, and Death itself is a condiment — who then truly knows where that (Self) is?

ws.e: the Brahmin class, priestly power — represents spiritual authority
the warrior class, temporal power — represents political authority
boiled rice, food — the Brahmin and Kshatriya are mere food for this power
condiment, sauce — something taken alongside the main food; Death is 'side-dish'
Death — even Death is consumed by this power
thus, truly — in this manner, as things really are

gr: brahma ca kṣatraṁ ca ubhe odanaḥ — 'Brahmin and warrior both are food': the two most powerful classes of Vedic society are mere nourishment for the Self/Brahman. mṛtyuḥ upasecanam — 'Death is a condiment': the most terrifying force in existence is reduced to a side-dish. ka itthā veda yatra saḥ — 'who truly knows where it is?': a rhetorical question expressing the Self's unfathomable transcendence.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.2.25 — The closing verse of Valli 2 ends with the most awe-inspiring image in the Katha: Death itself is a condiment for the Self. This is spoken by Yama — Death himself — who admits that even he is 'consumed' by the reality he is teaching about. The verse also appears in the Taittiriya Upanishad (2.8) and Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (5.2.2).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'ब्रह्म' और 'क्षत्र' सम्पूर्ण सृष्टि का प्रतीक हैं — आध्यात्मिक शक्ति और सांसारिक शक्ति दोनों ब्रह्म द्वारा 'खायी' जाती हैं, अर्थात् ब्रह्म में विलीन होती हैं। मृत्यु स्वयं ब्रह्म में विलीन है — मृत्यु भी मरती है।
advaita.en: Shankara reads 'brahma' and 'kṣatra' as symbols of the entire creation — spiritual and worldly power are both 'consumed' by Brahman, i.e., dissolved into Brahman. Death itself dissolves into Brahman — even Death dies.
advaita.ins: The ultimate reality devours everything — including death. When you know the Self, death loses its power because even Death is food for what you truly are.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् ही वह शक्ति हैं जिसके लिए सम्पूर्ण सृष्टि और मृत्यु भी भोजन-मात्र हैं। 'क इत्था वेद' — भगवान् की महिमा अगम्य है; केवल भक्ति से ही कुछ जाना जा सकता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord is the power for whom the entire creation and even Death are mere food. 'Ka itthā veda' — the Lord's glory is unfathomable; only through devotion can something be known.
vishisht.ins: The Lord's power makes even Death a trifle. When you take refuge in such a Lord, what remains to fear?

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द इसमें चेतना की सर्वोच्च शक्ति देखते हैं — जो शक्ति ब्राह्मण और क्षत्रिय को 'खा' सकती है और मृत्यु को चटनी बना सकती है, वह भौतिक, प्राणिक, और मानसिक सभी स्तरों से परे है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees the supreme power of consciousness — the power that can 'consume' both spiritual and temporal authority and make Death a condiment transcends the physical, vital, and mental planes.
aurobindo.ins: The ultimate consciousness is not afraid of death — it eats death for breakfast. This is not poetic exaggeration but a description of the supramental reality.

dp.q: 🔍 What does it mean that Death is a 'condiment' (upasecana)?
dp.a: The image of Death as upasecana (condiment, sauce, side-dish) is one of the most powerful in all Upanishadic literature. Consider the context: Yama, the Lord of Death, is speaking. He is telling Nachiketa about a reality so vast that even he himself — Death — is reduced to a condiment, a mere accompaniment to the main course. The main 'food' (odana) is the two most powerful forces in Vedic society: brahma (spiritual power) and kṣatra (temporal power). Together they represent everything that exists — religion and politics, temple and throne, priest and king. For the Self/Brahman, ALL of this is merely food — consumed, digested, absorbed. And Death? Death is not even the main dish — it is the side sauce. The implications are staggering: the most feared force in existence is trivial compared to the reality being described. When you know the Self, you do not merely 'overcome' death — you discover that death was always a minor detail in the larger scheme.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Valli 2 end with a question ('who knows where it is?')?
dp.a: The closing question 'ka itthā veda yatra saḥ' ('who truly knows where it is?') is deliberately open-ended. After an entire valli of teaching about the Self — its nature, its attributes, the means to know it — Yama ends with a confession of the Self's ultimate unknowability. This is not a contradiction but a statement of humility before the infinite. The Self has been described as 'subtler than the subtle, greater than the great,' 'bodiless among bodies,' 'neither born nor dying' — but these are all descriptions from the outside. The question 'who truly knows where it is?' points to the fact that the Self cannot be located (yatra = where) because it is not in space, and it cannot be fully known by an external knower because it IS the knower. The verse creates a productive tension: Yama has taught everything he can teach in words, and now the student must go beyond words to direct experience. The question is not despair but an invitation — it is the finger pointing at the moon, after which the student must look for themselves.
